Scotch whisky brands.Glenfiddich: Its name means valley of the deer in Gaelic, and its triangular green bottle holds one of the world's best-selling single malts.
Scotch whisky brands.Macallan: Aged mainly in sherry casks, this Speyside whisky holds auction records. A 1926 bottling sold for over a million pounds.
Scotch whisky brands.Laphroaig: Its peat-smoke, medicinal flavor is polarizing. Prince Charles granted it a royal warrant, an unusual honor for such a bold whisky.
Scotch whisky brands.Lagavulin: An Islay distillery, home to the 16-year-old malt that is smoky, rich, and long loved by peat lovers.
Scotch whisky brands.Johnnie Walker: The world's best-selling Scotch, with its striding man logo. Labels are named by color, like Red, Black, Green and Blue.
Scotch whisky brands.Glenlivet: Founded in 1824, it was the first Highland distillery to get a license after the 1823 Excise Act, to take smuggling out of Speyside.
Scotch whisky brands.Talisker: The only distillery on the Isle of Skye, famed for a briny, peppery taste of sea and spice.
Scotch whisky brands.Ardbeg: Another smoky Islay name, stocked with fans. Its Gaelic name and heavily peated style make it a cult favorite.
Scotch whisky brands.Chivas Regal: A blended Scotch that comes with an age statement, usually 12 years, and has long been a popular luxury gift.
Scotch whisky brands.Dewar's: Founded in Perth by John Dewar in 1846, it is a blended Scotch which uses a White Label and was a hit in America.
Scotch whisky brands.Highland Park: Distilled in Kirkwall on Orkney, it is among Scotland's northernmost distilleries, using local heather peat for gentle smoke and honey.
Scotch whisky brands.Balvenie: One of few distilleries that still grows its own barley and malts on site, alongside Glenfiddich in Dufftown.
Scotch whisky brands.Jack Daniel's: A Tennessee whiskey, made in Lynchburg and filtered through charcoal, so it is American, not Scotch.
Scotch whisky brands.Jim Beam: A Kentucky bourbon from a family distilling tradition over 200 years old. That makes it American whiskey.
Scotch whisky brands.Maker's Mark: Kentucky bourbon sealed with red wax. It uses soft red winter wheat rather than rye in its mash.
Scotch whisky brands.Jameson: Irish whiskey, from Dublin. Irish spelling includes an e, and it is typically triple-distilled for smoothness.
Scotch whisky brands.Bushmills: Northern Ireland's old distillery has a license dating to 1608, and it makes Irish whiskey rather than Scotch.
Scotch whisky brands.Wild Turkey: A Kentucky bourbon named after a hunting trip, which a distillery executive's hunting trip inspired, and it is American.
Scotch whisky brands.Crown Royal: A Canadian whisky, sold in a purple velvet bag and created for the 1939 royal visit of King George VI.
Scotch whisky brands.Suntory: A Japanese whisky house whose Yamazaki distillery opened in 1923, so this is Japan, not Scotland.
Scotch whisky brands.Yamazaki: Japan's first malt whisky distillery, built near Kyoto in 1923. Japanese, so it doesn't count as Scotch.
Scotch whisky brands.Bulleit: A Kentucky bourbon with high rye content, with a bottle whose label recalls frontier-era apothecary design.
Scotch whisky brands.Woodford Reserve: A Kentucky bourbon made in a distillery that is a National Historic Landmark and uses copper pot stills.
An Irish whiskey from County Offaly. The initials D.E.W. come from Daniel E. Williams, who ran the distillery.

Things used to thicken sauces.Cornstarch: Mixed with cold water first as a slurry, it thickens at about boiling, and gives a glossy finish, common in Chinese cooking.
Things used to thicken sauces.Flour: Wheat flour thickens when its starch swells in heat. It must be cooked a little first to avoid a raw taste.
Things used to thicken sauces.Arrowroot: A starch from tropical root plants that thickens at lower heat and stays clear and glossy, and it holds up well in acidic sauces.
Things used to thicken sauces.Roux: Equal parts fat and flour cooked together. The longer it cooks, the darker and nuttier it gets, but the less it thickens.
Things used to thicken sauces.Gelatin: A protein from collagen, which sets liquids into a gel as they cool, and gives pan sauces a silky body.
Things used to thicken sauces.Tapioca starch: Extracted from cassava root, it makes sauces glossy and stretchy. The same plant gives us bubble tea pearls.
Things used to thicken sauces.Xanthan gum: A bacteria-fermented polysaccharide that thickens even in tiny amounts, which is why a pinch goes a long way in gluten-free cooking.
Things used to thicken sauces.Agar: Made from red seaweed, agar sets firmer than gelatin and stays solid at room temperature. It is used where vegetarian gelling is needed.
Things used to thicken sauces.Potato starch: Thickens at low temperatures and gives clear, glossy results, but it turns stringy if boiled hard.
Things used to thicken sauces.Egg yolk: Yolks thicken sauces such as custard or hollandaise as their proteins set gently. Overheat them and they scramble.
Things used to thicken sauces.Baking soda: Sodium bicarbonate releases carbon dioxide when it meets acid, so it leavens baking. It doesn't thicken a sauce.
Things used to thicken sauces.Yeast: Yeast ferments sugars into gas and flavor, making bread rise, not sauces thicken.
Things used to thicken sauces.Vinegar: An acid that adds tang and brightness. It can thin a sauce, and acids can even prevent thickening in a roux.
Things used to thicken sauces.Salt: It seasons and draws out moisture. It makes a sauce taste better but does not make it thicker.
Things used to thicken sauces.MSG: Monosodium glutamate boosts savoriness and umami without altering texture, so it won't thicken a sauce.
Things used to thicken sauces.Citric acid: This sour crystalline acid, abundant in citrus, adds tartness and acts as a preservative, but it has no thickening power.
Things used to thicken sauces.Lemon juice: Lemon juice adds acid and brightness. Acid can actually thin starch-thickened sauces, and it is not a thickener.
Things used to thicken sauces.Food coloring: It changes the look of a sauce but not its texture. A few drops are enough for vivid color.
Things used to thicken sauces.Vanilla extract: It's flavor only. Real vanilla extract is made by soaking vanilla pods in alcohol, and its flavor is complex.
Things used to thicken sauces.Cream of tartar: A byproduct of winemaking, it stabilizes whipped egg whites and keeps sugar from crystallizing, but doesn't thicken sauces.
Things used to thicken sauces.Baking powder: A mixture of baking soda and a dry acid, it makes batters rise. It doesn't thicken sauces.
Things used to thicken sauces.Water: Water thins sauces. Cooks often use it to adjust a sauce that has become too thick.
Things used to thicken sauces.Soy sauce: A salty fermented liquid that adds umami and color, but it is thin and does not thicken anything.
Things used to thicken sauces.Black pepper: It gives heat and aroma. Its piperine adds bite but no body, so it won't thicken a sauce.

Sea creatures that aren't fish.Starfish: Also called sea stars, they are echinoderms with no brain or blood. Many can regrow a lost arm.
Sea creatures that aren't fish.Jellyfish: Mostly water, with no brain, heart or bones. Jellyfish have been drifting in oceans for over 500 million years.
Sea creatures that aren't fish.Cuttlefish: A cephalopod that changes skin colour in a flash. Its internal cuttlebone helps it control buoyancy.
Sea creatures that aren't fish.Octopus: An invertebrate with three hearts, nine brains in a sense, and blue blood. It is not a fish at all.
Sea creatures that aren't fish.Squid: A mollusc with ten arms. The giant squid has the largest eyes in the animal kingdom, as big as dinner plates.
Sea creatures that aren't fish.Dolphin: A dolphin is a mammal that breathes air and nurses its young. It looks like a fish but isn't one.
Sea creatures that aren't fish.Whale: Whales are mammals and breathe air through blowholes. The blue whale is the biggest animal ever known.
Sea creatures that aren't fish.Seal: A marine mammal with flippers. Seals give birth and nurse pups on land or ice, so they are not fish.
Sea creatures that aren't fish.Crab: A crustacean with a hard exoskeleton. Crabs walk sideways because of how their legs are hinged.
Sea creatures that aren't fish.Lobster: A crustacean that lives on the seabed. It was once so common in New England that it was fed to prisoners.
Sea creatures that aren't fish.Sea urchin: A spiny echinoderm that moves on tiny tube feet. Its mouth is a complex jaw called Aristotle's lantern.
Sea creatures that aren't fish.Sea turtle: A reptile that spends life at sea, and females come ashore to lay eggs on beaches. It is not a fish.
Sea creatures that aren't fish.Coral: A coral reef is built by tiny animals called polyps, not plants. They are related to jellyfish.
Sea creatures that aren't fish.Seahorse: A trap: despite its name and shape, it is a fish, with gills and fins. The male carries the eggs and gives birth.
Sea creatures that aren't fish.Shark: A fish with a cartilage skeleton and gills. Sharks are older than trees, dating back over 400 million years.
Sea creatures that aren't fish.Eel: A snakelike fish, with gills. The electric eel is actually a knifefish, not a true eel.
Sea creatures that aren't fish.Stingray: A flat fish related to sharks, with a cartilage skeleton. It has a venomous barb on its tail.
Sea creatures that aren't fish.Clownfish: A fish that lives among sea anemone tentacles without being stung. All are born male, and the dominant one can become female.
Sea creatures that aren't fish.Swordfish: A large fish with a long bill, which it slashes through schools of prey. It is a fast swimmer, so definitely a fish.
Sea creatures that aren't fish.Pufferfish: A fish that inflates into a ball when threatened. Some species have a poison that is far stronger than cyanide.
Sea creatures that aren't fish.Tuna: A fast ocean fish that can swim at over 60 km/h. It is definitely a fish, with gills and scales.
Sea creatures that aren't fish.Anglerfish: A deep-sea fish with a glowing lure that attracts prey. In some species the tiny male fuses onto the female.
Sea creatures that aren't fish.Barracuda: A long, fast, toothy fish. It is a true fish, with gills and scales, and is a fierce reef predator.
Sea creatures that aren't fish.Manta ray: A giant filter-feeding fish with the biggest brain of any fish. Its cartilage skeleton marks it as a shark relative.

Animals whose babies are called cubs.Lion: A lion cub's spots fade as it grows. Lions are the only cats where males and females look so different, thanks to the male's mane.
Animals whose babies are called cubs.Tiger: Tiger cubs are born blind and are raised by the mother alone. Every tiger's stripe pattern is unique, even on its skin.
Animals whose babies are called cubs.Bear: Bear cubs are tiny at birth, often weighing less than a kilogram, born in winter dens while the mother hibernates.
Animals whose babies are called cubs.Leopard: Leopard cubs are born with their eyes closed, and the mother moves them between hiding places to protect them from predators.
Animals whose babies are called cubs.Cheetah: Cheetah cubs have a fluffy grey mane called a mantle, which may help them mimic the fierce honey badger and avoid predators.
Animals whose babies are called cubs.Panda: A newborn giant panda is pink, hairless, and about 1/900th the size of its mother, among the biggest size gaps of any mammal.
Animals whose babies are called cubs.Polar bear: Polar bear cubs are born in snow dens and weigh about 600 grams, roughly the size of a guinea pig.
Animals whose babies are called cubs.Jaguar: Jaguar cubs stay with their mother for up to two years. Jaguars have the most powerful bite of all big cats relative to size.
Animals whose babies are called cubs.Fox: Fox young are also called kits or pups, but cub is accepted too. Kits are born with dark fur and sealed eyes in a den.
Animals whose babies are called cubs.Horse: A baby horse is a foal. Within hours of birth, a foal can stand and run, a survival trait for a prey animal.
Animals whose babies are called cubs.Cow: A cow's baby is a calf. Cows have nearly 360-degree vision, though they have a blind spot directly behind them.
Animals whose babies are called cubs.Kangaroo: A baby kangaroo is a joey, not a cub. Newborn joeys are tiny and crawl unaided into the pouch.
Animals whose babies are called cubs.Goat: Baby goats are called kids, and the word became slang for children. Goats have rectangular pupils.
Animals whose babies are called cubs.Deer: A baby deer is a fawn, and its spots camouflage it. Fawns have almost no scent, to avoid predators.
Animals whose babies are called cubs.Swan: A baby swan is a cygnet. Cygnets often ride on a parent's back and can swim within hours of hatching.
Animals whose babies are called cubs.Sheep: A baby sheep is a lamb. A lamb can recognise its mother's bleat among a flock within days of birth.
Animals whose babies are called cubs.Pig: A baby pig is a piglet. Piglets compete for specific teats and tend to return to the same one for feeding.
Animals whose babies are called cubs.Owl: A baby owl is an owlet. Owlets often leave the nest before they can fly, climbing around on branches.
Animals whose babies are called cubs.Eagle: A baby eagle is an eaglet. Bald eagles build some of the largest nests of any bird, weighing over a tonne.
Animals whose babies are called cubs.Frog: A baby frog is a tadpole, not a cub. It starts out with gills and a tail and later grows legs.
Animals whose babies are called cubs.Goose: A baby goose is a gosling. Goslings can walk, swim and feed themselves within a day of hatching.
Animals whose babies are called cubs.Dog: Puppies are the name for baby dogs, not cubs, though wolf babies are sometimes called cubs. Puppies are born deaf and blind.
Animals whose babies are called cubs.Cat: A baby cat is a kitten. Domestic kittens are not cubs, but big-cat babies like lion and tiger young are.
Animals whose babies are called cubs.Elephant: A baby elephant is a calf. It weighs around 100 kilograms at birth and its mother carries it for nearly two years.

Succulents.Aloe vera: Aloe vera stores soothing gel in its thick leaves, and it has been used for burns and skin care for thousands of years.
Succulents.Jade plant: The jade plant is a long-lived succulent that stores water in glossy oval leaves and can last for decades as a houseplant.
Succulents.Agave: Agaves store water in thick rosettes, and some bloom just once after years before dying; blue agave becomes tequila.
Succulents.Cactus: Cacti are succulents native to the Americas, and their spines are modified leaves that shade the plant and cut water loss.
Succulents.Echeveria: Echeveria forms neat rosettes of fleshy leaves, often tinted pink or blue, and comes from Mexico and Central America.
Succulents.Sedum: Sedums are tough succulents that grow on rocky ground and are common as groundcover and on green roofs.
Succulents.Haworthia: Haworthia are small, slow-growing succulents from South Africa, often with translucent windows on their leaves.
Succulents.Snake plant: Snake plants store water in stiff upright leaves and can go weeks without a drink, which is why they survive dim offices.
Succulents.Hens and chicks: Hens and chicks multiply by sending out little offsets around a mother rosette, like chicks around a hen.
Succulents.String of pearls: String of pearls trails long strands of bead-like leaves that store water, and it comes from southwestern Africa.
Succulents.Kalanchoe: Kalanchoe species grow tiny plantlets along their leaf edges, and some are sold as colorful flowering houseplants.
Succulents.Fern: Ferns prefer moist shade and have thin fronds that lose water quickly, so they're the opposite of succulents.
Succulents.Ivy: Ivy has thin, flat leaves and no water-storing tissue, so it isn't a succulent.
Succulents.Orchid: Orchids typically store water in thickened roots or bulbs, but they're not classed as succulents.
Succulents.Bamboo: Bamboo is a grass, with hollow canes and slim leaves, and not a water-storing plant.
Succulents.Fiddle-leaf fig: Fiddle-leaf figs have big, thin leaves and need regular watering, so they're no succulent.
Succulents.Pothos: Pothos is a trailing vine with ordinary leaves, famous for tolerating neglect, but not a water-storing plant.
Succulents.Peace lily: Peace lilies droop dramatically when thirsty, a sign they don't store water like succulents.
Succulents.Monstera: Monstera's big split leaves are thin, and it's a tropical climber rather than a succulent.
Succulents.Basil: Basil has soft, thin leaves that wilt quickly without water, so it's no succulent.
Succulents.Moss: Moss has no thick leaves and no true roots, and it soaks up water from the air and rain.
Succulents.Venus flytrap: The Venus flytrap is a carnivorous plant from a few boggy parts of the Carolinas, and it needs wet soil.
Succulents.Rubber plant: Rubber plants have thick, glossy leaves, but they come from the fig family and aren't true succulents.
Succulents.Philodendron: Philodendrons have thin, heart-shaped leaves and are tropical climbers, not succulents.

Leafy greens.Spinach: Popeye is credited with boosting US spinach sales in the 1930s, though the iron claim stems from a decimal myth.
Leafy greens.Kale: It becomes sweeter after a frost, as the plant turns starch into sugar, and was Europe's winter staple.
Leafy greens.Lettuce: A relative of the sunflower and daisy, and the word lettuce comes from Latin lac, for the milky sap.
Leafy greens.Arugula: Also called rocket in Britain, and it has a peppery bite.
Leafy greens.Chard: Swiss chard isn't from Switzerland: the name came to distinguish it from French varieties, and it's a beet relative.
Leafy greens.Collard greens: A Southern US staple, traditionally eaten on New Year's Day for luck and money.
Leafy greens.Watercress: Eaten since ancient times, it's very nutritious and grows in cold running water.
Leafy greens.Bok choy: The name is Cantonese for 'white vegetable', and its stalks are crisp and mild.
Leafy greens.Romaine: The lettuce of Caesar salad, a dish credited to Caesar Cardini in Tijuana in the 1920s.
Leafy greens.Endive: Belgian endive is grown in the dark so that it stays pale and slightly bitter.
Leafy greens.Radicchio: A red chicory with bitter leaves, and cooking it on the grill mellows the bitterness.
Leafy greens.Mustard greens: These come from the same plant species as mustard seed, and have a sharp, peppery bite.
Leafy greens.Iceberg: Named for the ice it was packed in for rail shipping across the US, and it is crunchy but low in nutrients.
Leafy greens.Broccoli: It's flower buds, not leaves, from a cabbage relative, so it's a florets vegetable.
Leafy greens.Asparagus: We eat the young shoots, which are stems, and not leaves.
Leafy greens.Celery: We eat the stalks, so not a leafy green, though the leaves are edible.
Leafy greens.Leek: Its pale part is a bundle of leaf bases and so it's more stem than leaf.
Leafy greens.Zucchini: A summer squash, so it is a fruit, not a leafy green.
Leafy greens.Green bean: Green beans are the immature seed pods of the plant, and they are not a leafy green. Haricots verts are the thin French type.
Leafy greens.Pea: We eat seeds, or the whole pod in snow peas, not leaves.
Leafy greens.Okra: A fruit pod from a mallow relative that becomes slimy when cooked.
Leafy greens.Artichoke: Only the flower bud of this thistle relative is eaten, so it's not a leafy green.
Leafy greens.Cucumber: A cucumber is a fruit, a gourd family member, and mostly water.
Leafy greens.Fennel: We eat the bulb, a base of overlapping leaf bases, but the fronds are an herb; mostly considered a vegetable.

Things made from coconut.Coconut milk: Squeezed from the grated flesh, not the liquid inside. The thick cream floats to the top of a standing can.
Things made from coconut.Desiccated coconut: Dried, finely shredded white flesh. It is a key ingredient in macaroons and Bounty bars.
Things made from coconut.Coconut flour: Flour made from the dried flesh left after coconut milk is pressed. It absorbs huge amounts of liquid and is gluten-free.
Things made from coconut.Piña colada: Puerto Rico's national drink, a blend of rum, pineapple and coconut cream. It was made official in 1978.
Things made from coconut.Coconut water: The clear liquid inside young green coconuts. It was used as emergency IV fluid in the Pacific in WWII.
Things made from coconut.Bounty: Coconut filling in milk chocolate, marketed in Britain as a taste of paradise. In the US, the dark chocolate version is called Mounds.
Things made from coconut.Haupia: A Hawaiian coconut milk pudding thickened with arrowroot or cornstarch. It is a luau staple and is cut into squares.
Things made from coconut.Coconut oil: Solid at cool room temperatures, since it is rich in saturated fat. It melts at around 24 C.
Things made from coconut.Mounds: Dark chocolate bar filled with sweet coconut, first sold in 1920. It has a sister bar, Almond Joy, which adds almonds.
Things made from coconut.Copra: Dried coconut kernel, the raw material that is pressed to make coconut oil. It was once a major trade good in the Pacific.
Things made from coconut.Macaron: A French almond meringue sandwich. Don't mix it up with the coconut macaroon, which has a similar name.
Things made from coconut.Marzipan: A paste of ground almonds and sugar. The lookalike taste has nothing to do with coconut.
Things made from coconut.Almond milk: Blended almonds and water. Many varieties are mostly water, with only a small percent almonds.
Things made from coconut.Oat milk: A drink made from oats. It was invented in Sweden in the 1990s by a scientist seeking an option for lactose-intolerant people.
Things made from coconut.Tapioca: Starch from cassava roots. It is chewy and neutral, often cooked in coconut milk but not made from it.
Things made from coconut.Palm oil: From the fruit of the oil palm tree, not the coconut palm. It is now in about half of packaged supermarket products.
Things made from coconut.Cashew butter: Ground cashews, which are seeds that hang beneath a fruit called the cashew apple.
Things made from coconut.Ghee: Clarified butter used in India. It's dairy fat, so no coconut is involved.
Things made from coconut.Tahini: Ground sesame seeds. It is the creamy base for hummus.
Things made from coconut.Mochi: Pounded glutinous rice. Its fillings can include coconut but the dough itself is rice.
Things made from coconut.Panna cotta: Italian for cooked cream, a dessert of cream set with gelatin. Coconut versions exist but the classic uses dairy.
Things made from coconut.Rice pudding: Rice simmered with milk and sugar. Some versions use coconut milk, but traditional ones use dairy.
Things made from coconut.Butterscotch: Brown sugar and butter. It has no coconut, just a caramel taste.
Things made from coconut.Nougat: Whipped egg whites or honey with nuts such as almonds. Its name probably comes from a Latin word for nut.

Cities in Mexico.Mexico City: Built on the drained bed of Lake Texcoco atop the Aztec capital Tenochtitlan, it is sinking in places by several centimeters a year.
Cities in Mexico.Guadalajara: Birthplace of mariachi music and tequila culture; the town of Tequila sits about an hour's drive northwest of this city.
Cities in Mexico.Monterrey: This northern industrial hub sits beneath the saddle-shaped Cerro de la Silla and is home to Mexico's steel and brewing giants.
Cities in Mexico.Cancún: Planners chose this spot by computer in the 1970s; it was nearly empty sandbar and jungle before the resort was built.
Cities in Mexico.Tijuana: One of the busiest land border crossings in the world is here, and the Caesar salad is claimed to have been invented in this city.
Cities in Mexico.Acapulco: Once the Pacific terminus of the Spanish Manila galleons, it later became a 1950s Hollywood playground famous for its cliff divers.
Cities in Mexico.Oaxaca: Called the land of seven moles, this southern city is a center of Zapotec culture, mezcal, and elaborate Day of the Dead festivities.
Cities in Mexico.Puebla: The 1862 victory over French forces here is what Cinco de Mayo celebrates, and it is more a local holiday than a national one.
Cities in Mexico.Tulum: Its Maya walled city perches on seaside cliffs; it was among the last cities the Maya built and was still inhabited when Spaniards arrived.
Cities in Mexico.Puerto Vallarta: A sleepy fishing village until John Huston filmed The Night of the Iguana nearby in 1964, which made Elizabeth Taylor and Richard Burton's romance a tourist draw.
Cities in Mexico.Cabo San Lucas: Land's end of the Baja peninsula, where the Pacific meets the Gulf of California, marked by the rock arch known as El Arco.
Cities in Mexico.San Antonio: Trap: this city is in Texas, home of the Alamo, even though its Spanish name and Mexican heritage make it feel like it could belong south of the border.
Cities in Mexico.San Diego: Trap: it is a California city, though it sits right on the border and forms a huge binational metro area with Tijuana.
Cities in Mexico.El Paso: Trap: this Texas city faces Ciudad Juarez across the Rio Grande, and the two form one of the largest binational metro areas anywhere.
Cities in Mexico.Santa Fe: Trap: it is New Mexico's capital, founded around 1610, making it the oldest state capital in the US.
Cities in Mexico.Los Angeles: Trap: the Spanish name 'the Angels' fits, but it is in California; it is also home to one of the largest Mexican-origin populations outside Mexico.
Cities in Mexico.Havana: Trap: Cuba's capital, not Mexico's, famous for vintage American cars and its Spanish colonial old town.
Cities in Mexico.Bogotá: Trap: capital of Colombia, sitting at about 2,600 meters in the Andes, making it one of the highest big capitals in the world.
Cities in Mexico.Lima: Trap: Peru's capital, one of the driest big cities on Earth, gets almost no rain yet is cloaked in fog much of the year.
Cities in Mexico.Panama City: Trap: the capital of Panama, where skyscrapers rise next to the Pacific entrance of the Panama Canal.
Cities in Mexico.San José: Trap: capital of Costa Rica, a country that abolished its army in 1948 and put the money into schools instead.
Cities in Mexico.Tegucigalpa: Trap: Honduras's capital, whose name likely comes from a Nahuatl phrase often translated as silver hills.
Cities in Mexico.Guatemala City: Trap: the largest city in Central America, with no connection to Mexico except a long shared border to the north.
Cities in Mexico.Managua: Trap: capital of Nicaragua, on the shore of Lake Managua, and it was largely flattened by a 1972 earthquake.

Cities in Florida.Miami: The only major US city founded by a woman, Julia Tuttle, who persuaded a railroad to extend here after a freeze killed crops elsewhere in the state.
Cities in Florida.Orlando: Walt Disney quietly bought land here in the 1960s under dummy company names, which later became Walt Disney World.
Cities in Florida.Tampa: Cigar-making immigrants from Cuba and Spain built Ybor City here, and the Tampa Bay Buccaneers play in this city.
Cities in Florida.Jacksonville: By land area it is the largest city in the contiguous US, covering over 700 square miles.
Cities in Florida.Tallahassee: The state capital sits in the north near Georgia; its name comes from a Creek word often glossed as old fields or old town.
Cities in Florida.Key West: The southernmost point of the continental US is here, only about 90 miles from Cuba, and Ernest Hemingway lived here in the 1930s.
Cities in Florida.Fort Lauderdale: Its canals gave it the nickname Venice of America, and it was the original spring-break hub of the 1960 film Where the Boys Are.
Cities in Florida.Daytona Beach: Cars raced on its hard-packed sand in the early 1900s, which led to the Daytona 500, held at the speedway since 1959.
Cities in Florida.Pensacola: Founded by Spanish settlers in 1559, it is arguably the oldest European-settled place in the US, and it is the home of the Blue Angels.
Cities in Florida.Boca Raton: Its name means mouse's mouth in Spanish, and it is home to IBM's first personal computer, which was designed here in 1981.
Cities in Florida.Sarasota: Circus owner John Ringling made his winter headquarters here, and his art museum and mansion remain landmarks.
Cities in Florida.West Palm Beach: Henry Flagler built it as a service town for his rich Palm Beach hotel guests, and a short bridge still links the two.
Cities in Florida.Atlanta: Trap: Georgia's capital hosted the 1996 Olympics and is home to Coca-Cola, so it feels Southern but is not in Florida.
Cities in Florida.Savannah: Trap: Georgia's oldest city has a famous grid of 22 leafy squares laid out by General Oglethorpe in 1733.
Cities in Florida.Charleston: Trap: this South Carolina city is where the Civil War began, with shots fired on Fort Sumter in 1861.
Cities in Florida.New Orleans: Trap: Louisiana's jazz birthplace lies on the Gulf too, but across several states to the west of Florida's panhandle.
Cities in Florida.Mobile: Trap: Alabama's port city claims to have held America's first Mardi Gras, even before New Orleans.
Cities in Florida.Birmingham: Trap: Alabama's largest city was named for England's steel town, since iron and steel built its early fortunes.
Cities in Florida.Havana: Trap: Cuba's capital is only 90 miles from Key West but lies across the Florida Straits.
Cities in Florida.Nassau: Trap: the capital of The Bahamas, a former pirate base, sits on New Providence island, east of Florida.
Cities in Florida.Myrtle Beach: Trap: South Carolina's golf-and-boardwalk resort feels very Floridian, but it sits on the Grand Strand in the Carolinas.
Cities in Florida.Biloxi: Trap: Mississippi's Gulf Coast town is known for casinos and was the original home of the Biloxi tribe's name.
Cities in Florida.Charlotte: Trap: North Carolina's biggest city is the US's second-largest banking center, but it is not in Florida.
Cities in Florida.Montgomery: Trap: Alabama's capital is where Rosa Parks refused to give up her bus seat in 1955, sparking a boycott.

Part of the United Kingdom.England: The largest of the four nations, it holds around 84 percent of the UK's population, and the Union Jack mixes its St George's cross with Scotland's and Ireland's.
Part of the United Kingdom.Scotland: It voted in a 2014 referendum to stay in the UK, and its national animal is the unicorn.

Part of the United Kingdom.Northern Ireland: It has been part of the UK since Ireland's partition in 1921, and the Giant's Causeway is its famous basalt coast.
Part of the United Kingdom.London: The UK capital sits on the Thames and began as Roman Londinium around 43 AD.
Part of the United Kingdom.Cornwall: The pasty is the county's signature dish, and the county has its own Celtic language, Cornish, which was revived after nearly dying out.
Part of the United Kingdom.Yorkshire: England's largest historic county, it gave the world Yorkshire pudding, and locals are fiercely proud of its white rose emblem.
Part of the United Kingdom.Belfast: The Titanic was built in its shipyard, and the city is now the capital of Northern Ireland.
Part of the United Kingdom.Cardiff: The capital of Wales has a castle in the city center that began as a Roman fort.
Part of the United Kingdom.Isle of Wight: England's largest island lies just off the south coast, and its Needles chalk stacks are a landmark; Queen Victoria had a holiday home there.
Part of the United Kingdom.Shetland: Its islands are closer to Norway than to London, and the small, shaggy Shetland pony originates here.
Part of the United Kingdom.Orkney: Skara Brae, a Stone Age village here, is older than Stonehenge and the Egyptian pyramids.

Part of the United Kingdom.Jersey: Trap: a Crown Dependency, not in the UK, and the breed of cattle was named after it.
Part of the United Kingdom.Guernsey: Trap: another Crown Dependency, not part of the UK, famous for its cattle breed and the Literary and Potato Peel Pie Society.
Part of the United Kingdom.Gibraltar: Trap: a British Overseas Territory at the southern tip of Spain, which is separate from the UK itself.
Part of the United Kingdom.Falkland Islands: Trap: a British Overseas Territory in the South Atlantic, and Argentina and Britain fought a war over them in 1982.
Part of the United Kingdom.Bermuda: Trap: a British Overseas Territory in the North Atlantic, and the Bermuda Triangle named after it is more legend than fact.
Part of the United Kingdom.Dublin: Trap: the capital of the Republic of Ireland, which left the UK in 1922.
Part of the United Kingdom.Cork: Trap: the Republic of Ireland's second city, and not part of the UK, though the name sounds English.
Part of the United Kingdom.Calais: Trap: the French port closest to England, only about 21 miles across the Channel from Dover.
Part of the United Kingdom.Normandy: Trap: a French region, but William the Conqueror from there took England in 1066.
Part of the United Kingdom.Brittany: Trap: a French region with Celtic roots, and its name comes from Britons who fled there.
Part of the United Kingdom.Galway: Trap: a city on Ireland's west coast, in the Republic, which is not part of the UK.

US national parks.Yellowstone: The first national park in the world, founded in 1872, sits atop a supervolcano and holds about half of the world's geysers, including Old Faithful.
US national parks.Yosemite: Famous for El Capitan and Half Dome, its granite cliffs are a world climbing destination, and Ansel Adams made it famous in photographs.
US national parks.Grand Canyon: The Colorado River carved it about 450 kilometres long and up to 1.8 kilometres deep, exposing nearly two billion years of rock.
US national parks.Zion: Utah's park of towering sandstone cliffs, where hikers wade through the Virgin River in The Narrows.
US national parks.Arches: Utah's park holds over 2,000 natural sandstone arches, the greatest concentration in the world.
US national parks.Glacier: A Montana park near the Canadian border, with glaciers shrinking rapidly, and its Going-to-the-Sun Road crosses the Continental Divide.
US national parks.Acadia: A Maine park where Cadillac Mountain is among the first places in the US to see the sunrise for part of the year.
US national parks.Everglades: A vast subtropical wetland in Florida that's the only place where alligators and crocodiles live together.
US national parks.Denali: Alaska's park contains North America's tallest peak at about 6,190 metres, once called Mount McKinley.
US national parks.Olympic: A Washington park that packs glaciers, a temperate rainforest and rocky coast into a single place.
US national parks.Joshua Tree: California's park where two deserts meet, with the twisted trees named by Mormon settlers who thought they looked like Joshua with arms raised.
US national parks.Bryce Canyon: Utah's park has the world's largest collection of hoodoos, tall rock spires, which glow orange at sunrise.
US national parks.Death Valley: Furnace Creek once recorded 134 degrees Fahrenheit in 1913, the hottest air temperature ever reliably measured on Earth.
US national parks.Banff: Canada's oldest national park, in the Rockies of Alberta, so it's not American.
US national parks.Mount Rushmore: A national memorial, not a park, with 18-metre faces of four presidents, carved by sculptor Gutzon Borglum.
US national parks.Statue of Liberty: A national monument, a gift from France in 1886, not a national park, and its inner frame came from Gustave Eiffel.
US national parks.Niagara Falls: Famous for its three waterfalls, it is a state park on the US side and a Canadian park on the other, not a national park.
US national parks.Lake Tahoe: A huge, clear alpine lake on the California-Nevada border, which is a state and national forest area, not a national park.
US national parks.Monument Valley: A Navajo Tribal Park on the Utah-Arizona border, with sandstone buttes from many Westerns, not a national park.
US national parks.Hoover Dam: A concrete arch dam on the Colorado River, completed in 1936, and part of a national recreation area, not a national park.
US national parks.Central Park: New York's 843-acre city park is run by a conservancy, not part of the National Park system.
US national parks.Kruger: South Africa's famed national park, home to the Big Five, is far from the US.
US national parks.Serengeti: Tanzania's plains hold an annual migration of over a million wildebeest, so it belongs to Africa.
US national parks.Muir Woods: A national monument north of San Francisco with old-growth coastal redwoods, not a national park.

Waters around Australia.Pacific Ocean: The Pacific Ocean borders Australia's east coast, and holds the Great Barrier Reef.
Waters around Australia.Gulf of Carpentaria: This shallow gulf in the north is the home of the 'Morning Glory', a rare rolling cloud that can stretch across the sky.
Waters around Australia.Bass Strait: Bass Strait separates Tasmania from the mainland, with rough seas, and is named after surgeon George Bass.
Waters around Australia.Java Sea: The Java Sea lies north of Java in Indonesia, not Australia; the Timor and Arafura seas are closer.
Waters around Australia.South China Sea: The South China Sea is bounded by China and Southeast Asia and is far to the north of Australia.
Waters around Australia.Red Sea: The Red Sea lies between Africa and Arabia, thousands of kilometers from Australia.
Waters around Australia.Arabian Sea: The Arabian Sea is part of the northern Indian Ocean, off India and Arabia, not Australia.
Waters around Australia.Bering Sea: The Bering Sea lies between Alaska and Russia in the far north.
Waters around Australia.Caribbean Sea: The Caribbean Sea belongs to the Atlantic, on the other side of the world.
Waters around Australia.Sea of Okhotsk: The Sea of Okhotsk is a cold Russian sea that freezes in winter, nowhere near Australia.
Waters around Australia.Philippine Sea: The Philippine Sea lies east of the Philippines and does not touch Australia.
Waters around Australia.Andaman Sea: The Andaman Sea lies off Myanmar and Thailand, in the northeast Indian Ocean.
Waters around Australia.Celebes Sea: The Celebes Sea sits between Sulawesi and the southern Philippines, north of Australia.
Waters around Australia.Black Sea: The Black Sea is bordered by Turkey, Ukraine and Russia, and it is almost fully landlocked.
Waters around Australia.Baltic Sea: The Baltic Sea in northern Europe is brackish, much less salty than the ocean.
Waters around Australia.Ross Sea: The Ross Sea is in Antarctica, not around Australia, and is the southernmost sea on Earth.
Waters around Australia.Yellow Sea: The Yellow Sea off China and Korea gets its name from the sediment colouring its waters.
Waters around Australia.Weddell Sea: The Weddell Sea in Antarctica is where Shackleton's ship Endurance was crushed by ice in 1915.

Moons of Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus or Nept.Europa: Beneath Europa's icy shell lies a salty ocean with more water than Earth's seas, which makes it a top place to look for life.
Moons of Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus or Nept.Ganymede: Ganymede is the largest moon in the solar system and the only moon with its own magnetic field.
Moons of Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus or Nept.Callisto: Callisto is one of the most heavily cratered surfaces known, a record of ancient impacts.
Moons of Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus or Nept.Titan: Titan has a thick nitrogen atmosphere and methane lakes; the Huygens probe landed on it in 2005.
Moons of Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus or Nept.Enceladus: Enceladus shoots geysers of water ice from its south pole that feed Saturn's E ring.
Moons of Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus or Nept.Mimas: Mimas has a giant crater, Herschel, that makes it look like the Death Star from Star Wars.
Moons of Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus or Nept.Rhea: Rhea is Saturn's second-largest moon, a heavily cratered ball of mostly water ice.
Moons of Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus or Nept.Iapetus: Iapetus is two-toned, one side dark as coal and the other bright, with an enormous ridge along its equator.
Moons of Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus or Nept.Titania: Titania, Uranus's largest moon, is named for the fairy queen in Shakespeare's A Midsummer Night's Dream.
Moons of Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus or Nept.Oberon: Oberon is named for Titania's husband in the same play, and both moons were found by William Herschel in 1787.
Moons of Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus or Nept.Miranda: Miranda is a patchwork moon of Uranus with enormous cliffs, perhaps the tallest in the solar system.
Moons of Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus or Nept.Triton: Triton orbits Neptune backward and erupts nitrogen geysers, likely a captured Kuiper Belt object.
Moons of Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus or Nept.Phobos: Phobos orbits Mars so close that it may break apart or crash into the planet in tens of millions of years.
Moons of Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus or Nept.Deimos: Deimos is tiny, only about 12 km across, and orbits Mars, not a giant planet.
Moons of Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus or Nept.Charon: Charon is Pluto's moon, big enough that they orbit a point in space between them.
Moons of Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus or Nept.Ceres: Ceres is a dwarf planet in the asteroid belt, not a moon.
Moons of Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus or Nept.Pallas: Pallas is a large asteroid discovered in 1802, orbiting the Sun itself.
Moons of Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus or Nept.Eris: Eris is a dwarf planet and has its own small moon, Dysnomia.
Moons of Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus or Nept.The Moon: The Moon is Earth's own moon, not one of the giant planets'.
Moons of Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus or Nept.Halley's Comet: Halley's Comet circles the Sun every 76 years or so and is no moon.
Moons of Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus or Nept.Sedna: Sedna is a distant icy world taking roughly 11,000 years to orbit the Sun.
Moons of Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus or Nept.Mars: Mars is a planet, and its only moons are Phobos and Deimos.
Moons of Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus or Nept.Vesta: Vesta is a big asteroid in the main belt, visited by the Dawn probe in 2011; it orbits the Sun, not a giant planet.

Alloys (metal mixtures).Bronze: A mix of mostly copper with tin, it was strong enough to name an age. Bells and statues are still cast from it.
Alloys (metal mixtures).Brass: Copper plus zinc. It's used for musical instruments partly because it carries sound well, and its gold color varies with the zinc content.
Alloys (metal mixtures).Steel: Iron with a little carbon, usually under 2 percent. Adding chromium makes stainless steel, which resists rust.
Alloys (metal mixtures).Pewter: Mostly tin with a bit of copper or antimony. Old pewter with lead could leach into drinks, so modern pewter is lead-free.
Alloys (metal mixtures).Solder: A low-melting metal alloy, traditionally tin and lead, used to join electronics. Today most is lead-free.
Alloys (metal mixtures).Sterling silver: Contains 92.5 percent silver, with the rest usually copper for strength. Pure silver is too soft for cutlery and jewelry.
Alloys (metal mixtures).White gold: Gold mixed with white metals such as nickel or palladium, often coated in rhodium for shine. It is a pale alloy, not a separate element.
Alloys (metal mixtures).Rose gold: Its pink tint comes from copper mixed into the gold. The more copper, the redder it gets.
Alloys (metal mixtures).Electrum: A natural gold-silver alloy found in rivers. The Lydians used it to make some of the first coins, around 600 BCE.
Alloys (metal mixtures).Cast iron: Iron with over 2 percent carbon, which makes it hard and brittle but good at holding heat. That's why skillets are made from it.
Alloys (metal mixtures).Amalgam: Any alloy containing mercury. Dental fillings were long made of silver amalgam, and mercury lets it set at room temperature.
Alloys (metal mixtures).Copper: A trap: it is a pure element, not an alloy. It was among the first metals used by humans, over 10,000 years ago.
Alloys (metal mixtures).Tin: A pure element that, mixed with copper, makes bronze. The 'tin cans' we know are actually steel with a thin tin coating.
Alloys (metal mixtures).Zinc: A pure element, though it makes brass when mixed with copper. It also coats steel to prevent rust, called galvanizing.
Alloys (metal mixtures).Iron: A pure element. It becomes steel only when carbon is added, so the metal itself isn't an alloy.
Alloys (metal mixtures).Aluminum: The most plentiful metal in Earth's crust, and a pure element. It was once rarer than gold, until electrolysis made it cheap.
Alloys (metal mixtures).Gold: A pure element in its 24-karat form. Jewelry is usually alloyed because pure gold is very soft.
Alloys (metal mixtures).Silver: The pure element has the highest electrical conductivity of any metal. It becomes sterling only once copper is added.
Alloys (metal mixtures).Nickel: A pure element. A US 'nickel' coin is mostly copper, with about a quarter nickel.
Alloys (metal mixtures).Lead: A pure, dense element, and not an alloy. It was once added to paint and gasoline, and both uses are now banned.
Alloys (metal mixtures).Titanium: A pure element as strong as steel yet far lighter. It's often alloyed for aircraft, but the metal itself is not an alloy.
Alloys (metal mixtures).Platinum: A pure element, rarer than gold. Jewelry platinum is often an alloy, but the metal itself is elemental.
Alloys (metal mixtures).Tungsten: A pure element with the highest melting point of any metal, over 3,400 degrees Celsius, which is why it was used in bulb filaments.
Alloys (metal mixtures).Mercury: A pure element and the only metal liquid at room temperature. It forms amalgams, but alone is not an alloy.

Real names of body parts.Philtrum: The groove between nose and upper lip; a smooth, flat one can be a sign of fetal alcohol exposure, and its origin lies in embryonic fusion.
Real names of body parts.Uvula: Latin for 'little grape', this dangling tissue helps seal the nasal passage when you swallow, and it can vibrate in snoring.
Real names of body parts.Glabella: The smooth patch between the eyebrows; the word relates to 'glabrous', meaning hairless, and doctors use it as a skull landmark.
Real names of body parts.Lunula: The pale half-moon at the base of a fingernail, Latin for 'little moon'; the thumb's is usually the most visible.
Real names of body parts.Tragus: The small flap in front of the ear canal; its name comes from the Greek for 'goat', for the tufts of hair it can carry.
Real names of body parts.Hallux: The big toe, a Latin name; it bears much of your body weight as you push off with each step while walking.
Real names of body parts.Axilla: The armpit, from the Latin word for it, and the source of the word 'axillary'; it holds a dense cluster of lymph nodes.
Real names of body parts.Purlicue: The web between the outstretched thumb and index finger, an old Scottish word that has made its way into anatomy.
Real names of body parts.Canthus: The corner of the eye where the lids meet; each eye has an inner and an outer one, and tear ducts drain at the inner.
Real names of body parts.Nares: The nostrils, plural of naris; the word also names the openings that let air pass from the nose into the throat.
Real names of body parts.Septum: The wall between the nostrils; the Latin word for partition also names the wall dividing the heart, and it is often slightly off-centre.
Real names of body parts.Snorkelium: Sounds anatomical, but it is made up; a snorkel is a breathing tube, and the real nose parts are nares and septum.
Real names of body parts.Glomp: Not a body part, though real tiny skin structures called glomus bodies help regulate your temperature in fingers and toes.
Real names of body parts.Thumbulus: Made up; the thumb's actual Latin name is pollex, and it is the only finger with two bones, not three.
Real names of body parts.Kneecapula: Invented; the real kneecap is the patella, Latin for 'little plate', and it protects the knee joint.
Real names of body parts.Nosette: Not real; the real name for the point where forehead meets the bridge of the nose is the nasion, a skull landmark.
Real names of body parts.Elbowra: Invented; the 'funny bone' is not a bone but the ulnar nerve, which tingles when you knock it at the elbow.
Real names of body parts.Toemund: Invented; real toe bones are phalanges, two in the big toe and three in each of the others.
Real names of body parts.Wristle: Invented; the wrist actually has eight small bones called carpals, arranged in two rows.
Real names of body parts.Spleenix: Invented; the real spleen filters blood, helps your immune system and sits under the ribs, and you can survive without it.
Real names of body parts.Ankleton: Invented; the real ankle bone is the talus, from the Latin for 'ankle', and it transfers your weight to the foot.
Real names of body parts.Cheekle: Invented; the real cheekbone is the zygomatic bone, and its name comes from a Greek word for yoke, since it links skull bones.
Real names of body parts.Gizzardine: Invented; a gizzard is a bird's muscular grinding stomach, and humans have no such organ, though some birds swallow stones to help it.
Real names of body parts.Navelope: Invented; the real term for the belly button is the umbilicus, the scar where your umbilical cord once attached.

Children of Zeus.Heracles: Zeus's mortal son, whose Twelve Labors included capturing Cerberus; Hera hated him for being born of her husband's affair.
Children of Zeus.Perseus: Zeus came to his mother Danae as a shower of golden rain; Perseus grew up to behead Medusa.
Children of Zeus.Persephone: Zeus's daughter by Demeter, in most versions, she spends part of every year in the underworld as Hades's queen.
Children of Zeus.Minos: The king of Crete was Zeus's son by Europa, and later became a judge of the dead in the underworld.
Children of Zeus.Hebe: Zeus and Hera's daughter, goddess of youth, served nectar to the gods and later married Heracles.
Children of Zeus.Poseidon: A trap: he's Zeus's brother, not his son; they drew lots for the sky, sea, and underworld.
Children of Zeus.Hades: A trap: Zeus's older brother, who got the underworld in a draw, is a sibling, not a child.
Children of Zeus.Hera: A trap: Zeus's wife was also his sister, and so a sibling, not a daughter; she mothered Ares and Hebe by him.
Children of Zeus.Demeter: A trap: this grain goddess is Zeus's sister, and mother of Persephone by him, rather than his daughter.
Children of Zeus.Hestia: A trap: the hearth goddess was Zeus's eldest sister and swore never to marry, so she's no child of his.
Children of Zeus.Cronus: A trap: Zeus's father, the Titan who swallowed his children, is not his child.
Children of Zeus.Rhea: A trap: Zeus's mother hid him on Crete and tricked Cronus into swallowing a rock.
Children of Zeus.Prometheus: The Titan who stole fire for humans; he was Zeus's cousin, not his son, and suffered an eagle eating his liver.
Children of Zeus.Atlas: A Titan condemned to hold up the sky, not a child of Zeus; atlas maps were named after him in the 1500s.
Children of Zeus.Achilles: A trap: his mother Thetis was a sea nymph and his father Peleus a mortal king, so he's no child of Zeus.
Children of Zeus.Theseus: A trap: this Athenian hero was son of King Aegeus, or in some tellings Poseidon, but never of Zeus.
Children of Zeus.Odysseus: A trap: the king of Ithaca was a mortal son of Laertes, though Athena favored him; he's no child of Zeus.
Children of Zeus.Medusa: A trap: the snake-haired Gorgon was a daughter of the sea gods Phorcys and Ceto, not of Zeus.

Instruments played in medieval Europe.Lute: Arriving through Moorish Spain from the Arab oud, it became the favorite instrument for songs and dance, and its name comes from al-ud.
Instruments played in medieval Europe.Harp: Small harps were widespread across medieval Europe, particularly in Ireland and Wales, and bardic traditions were built around them.
Instruments played in medieval Europe.Hurdy-gurdy: A hand crank rubs a wheel against the strings, so it sounds like a droning violin, and it was used in churches and later by street musicians.
Instruments played in medieval Europe.Recorder: This whistle flute was popular throughout the Middle Ages and Renaissance. Henry VIII owned dozens of them.
Instruments played in medieval Europe.Bagpipes: They were common in many parts of medieval Europe, not just Scotland, and appear in carvings and manuscripts across the continent.
Instruments played in medieval Europe.Psaltery: A flat box with strings plucked or struck, it was the ancestor of the harpsichord and was often shown played by angels.
Instruments played in medieval Europe.Shawm: A loud double-reed ancestor of the oboe, it was used for outdoor dances and ceremonies in town bands.
Instruments played in medieval Europe.Rebec: A small bowed, pear-shaped string instrument brought from the Islamic world, and an early ancestor of the violin family.
Instruments played in medieval Europe.Dulcimer: The hammered kind, struck with small mallets, was known in medieval Europe, and it is a distant relative of the piano.
Instruments played in medieval Europe.Pipe organ: Organs were in use in medieval churches, and some early ones needed several men to pump the bellows.
Instruments played in medieval Europe.Tabor: A small drum hung from the arm and struck with one hand, usually paired with a three-hole pipe played by the same performer.
Instruments played in medieval Europe.Saxophone: Trap: Adolphe Sax patented it in 1846, so it is a 19th-century invention.
Instruments played in medieval Europe.Electric guitar: Trap: it appeared in the 1930s, once amplifiers made guitars loud enough, so far too modern.
Instruments played in medieval Europe.Piano: Trap: Bartolomeo Cristofori made the first around 1700 in Italy, a few centuries after the medieval period.
Instruments played in medieval Europe.Clarinet: Trap: invented around 1700 in Germany by Johann Denner, so not medieval.
Instruments played in medieval Europe.Synthesizer: Trap: electronic synthesizers came in the 1960s, with Moog making them popular.
Instruments played in medieval Europe.Tuba: Trap: patented in Prussia in 1835, a thoroughly modern brass instrument.
Instruments played in medieval Europe.Harmonica: Trap: the free-reed mouth organ appeared in the early 1820s in Europe, so it is a modern instrument.
Instruments played in medieval Europe.Accordion: Trap: patented in Vienna in 1829, so it is a 19th-century invention.
Instruments played in medieval Europe.Theremin: Trap: Soviet inventor Leon Theremin created this played-without-touching instrument in 1920.
Instruments played in medieval Europe.Ukulele: Trap: it was developed in Hawaii in the 1880s from small Portuguese guitars, so well after medieval Europe.
Instruments played in medieval Europe.Drum machine: Trap: electronic rhythm machines date to the mid-20th century, and the Roland TR-808 helped shape hip-hop.
Instruments played in medieval Europe.Sousaphone: Trap: named for bandleader John Philip Sousa, who inspired it in the 1890s, so it is a late-1800s marching tuba.
Instruments played in medieval Europe.Kazoo: Trap: this buzzing toy instrument, associated with the 1840s American South, is far from medieval Europe.
