Things made of paper.Newspaper: Old newsprint is often made with recycled fiber and is cheap enough that it has long served as packing and fish-wrapping material.
Things made of paper.Paper towel: Paper towels began in 1907 as a way to cut germ spread in schools, and later became a kitchen staple in the 1930s.
Things made of paper.Toilet paper: Commercial toilet paper appeared in the US in 1857, and for a long time it was sold in flat packs, not rolls.
Things made of paper.Origami crane: Folding 1,000 paper cranes is said to grant a wish in Japanese tradition, and it became a symbol of peace after Sadako Sasaki's story.
Things made of paper.Sticky note: The weak glue came from a failed super-strong adhesive experiment at 3M, which a colleague later used to hold hymnal bookmarks.
Things made of paper.Coffee filter: The paper coffee filter was invented in 1908 by a German housewife, Melitta Bentz, who used blotting paper from her son's notebook.
Things made of paper.Paper bag: A machine that made flat-bottomed paper bags was invented by Margaret Knight in the 1870s, and her design is still in use.
Things made of paper.Paperback book: Cheap paperbacks surged in the 1930s with Penguin Books, whose first batch sold at the price of a pack of cigarettes.
Things made of paper.Tissue: Facial tissues began in 1924 as a way to remove cold cream, and only later did people start using them for sneezes.
Things made of paper.Bubble wrap: It's plastic, not paper. Bubble wrap began as a failed textured wallpaper, and was later sold as protective packing.
Things made of paper.Aluminum foil: It's metal, not paper. Foil is rolled so thin that the shiny side comes from being milled against a polished roller.
Things made of paper.Plastic wrap: It's plastic, not paper. It clings thanks to static charge, and modern versions are often polyethylene rather than the older PVC.
Things made of paper.Credit card: It looks like card stock, but credit cards are typically made of PVC plastic, not paper, for durability.
Things made of paper.Sponge: Most kitchen sponges are made of cellulose or polyurethane foam rather than paper, even though they soak up liquid just as well.
Things made of paper.Tea towel: It's cloth, usually cotton or linen, not paper. Linen tea towels were once preferred because they leave little lint on glasses.
Things made of paper.Balloon: It's latex or foil, not paper. Latex balloons come from rubber tree sap, and a thin one pops from stretching its walls past its limit.
Things made of paper.Rubber band: It's rubber, not paper. The rubber band was patented in England in 1845 by Stephen Perry.
Things made of paper.Glass jar: It's glass, made mostly of sand, and unlike paper it can be recycled over and over without losing quality.
Things made of paper.Cork: It's tree bark, not paper. Cork is harvested from cork oak trees without cutting them down, and the bark regrows.
Things made of paper.Tin can: It's steel with a thin tin coating, not paper. Most cans were once sealed with solder, which was a lead hazard.
Things made of paper.Shower curtain: It's plastic or fabric, not paper. The first shower curtains were sold to keep water in the tub, around the late 1800s.

Things that have a filter.Coffee maker: A paper filter holds back grounds and also traps oily compounds called diterpenes that can nudge up cholesterol.
Things that have a filter.Vacuum cleaner: HEPA filters in vacuums trap 99.97 percent of particles as small as 0.3 microns, which includes pollen and pet dander.
Things that have a filter.Air purifier: Many air purifiers pair a HEPA filter with a carbon one; the carbon soaks up smells that the HEPA part cannot catch.
Things that have a filter.Range hood: Range hoods often use a metal mesh filter that catches grease, which you can wash in the dishwasher.
Things that have a filter.Aquarium: An aquarium filter is a home for helpful bacteria that turn toxic fish waste into much less harmful compounds.
Things that have a filter.Water filter jug: Jugs use activated carbon, whose pores are so tiny that one gram has the surface area of a tennis court.
Things that have a filter.Swimming pool: A pool filter, often sand, can cycle the entire pool's water every 6 to 8 hours to keep it clear.
Things that have a filter.Air conditioner: A clogged air conditioner filter makes the unit work harder and can freeze the coils, so it should be cleaned regularly.
Things that have a filter.Tumble dryer: The dryer's lint trap catches fibers shed from clothes, and a clogged one is a leading cause of dryer fires.
Things that have a filter.Dishwasher: Dishwashers have a filter at the bottom that catches food bits; it needs cleaning occasionally or dishes come out grimy.
Things that have a filter.Car engine: An engine has an oil filter, an air filter and a fuel filter, each a thin barrier against grit that would wear parts out.
Things that have a filter.Toaster: A toaster has heating wires and a crumb tray but no filter; the tray simply catches fallen crumbs.
Things that have a filter.Stapler: A stapler is a simple spring-loaded lever with a strip of staples, no filter in sight.
Things that have a filter.Desk lamp: A desk lamp makes light and has no filter, though some lamps are fitted with a diffuser to soften glare.
Things that have a filter.Bookcase: A bookcase is just shelves; any dust filtering is done by the books themselves, mostly by collecting dust.
Things that have a filter.Doorbell: A doorbell has a button and a chime, with no filter at all; wired ones use a tiny transformer.
Things that have a filter.Wall clock: Clocks count time and need no filter, though a clock's escapement or a quartz crystal is its true heart.
Things that have a filter.Pencil: A pencil has no filter, and its lead is graphite mixed with clay, not lead.
Things that have a filter.Mirror: A mirror is glass backed with a thin silver or aluminum coating that reflects light and filters nothing.
Things that have a filter.Rolling pin: A rolling pin is a plain cylinder of wood or marble that flattens dough and filters nothing.
Things that have a filter.Hammer: A hammer is a solid head on a handle and has no filter or moving parts to clog.
Things that have a filter.Electric blanket: An electric blanket has heating wires woven into the fabric but nothing that filters.
Things that have a filter.Typewriter: A typewriter strikes ink through a ribbon straight to paper, so there is no filtering, only a ribbon that wears out.
Things that have a filter.Hair straightener: A hair straightener has heated plates and no filter; ceramic plates distribute the heat more evenly.

Things that stretch.Rubber band: The rubber band was patented in England in 1845 by Stephen Perry, a businessman whose firm made rubber products.
Things that stretch.Balloon: Latex balloons can stretch to several times their size, but the rubber grows thinner as it inflates, until it pops.
Things that stretch.Slime: Classic slime is a cross-linked polymer, usually white glue plus an activator, which is why it stretches then snaps if pulled fast.
Things that stretch.Bungee cord: Jump cords are bundles of rubber strands in a sheath, and modern bungee began in 1979 with Oxford students leaping from Bristol's Clifton Bridge.
Things that stretch.Leggings: Their stretch comes from spandex, also called elastane or Lycra, invented at DuPont in 1958 by chemist Joseph Shivers.
Things that stretch.Chewing gum: Gum base was once chicle, sap of the sapodilla tree, and today it is mostly synthetic polymers that stretch like rubber.
Things that stretch.Resistance band: Elastic bands were used in physical therapy long before gyms, because the tension grows smoothly as you stretch them.
Things that stretch.Plastic wrap: Cling film stretches thin to hug a bowl, and its ancestor, Saran, was discovered by accident in 1933 by a Dow lab worker.
Things that stretch.Hair tie: Most hair ties are a loop of elastic wrapped in fabric, and the elastic can stretch many times its resting size.
Things that stretch.Tights: When nylon stockings reached American stores in 1940, they caused a buying frenzy and sold in the millions within months.
Things that stretch.Pizza dough: Kneading builds gluten, a stretchy protein net, which is why dough must rest before it can be tossed thin without tearing.
Things that stretch.Melted mozzarella: Mozzarella is a pasta filata, or spun paste, cheese: its protein strands are aligned by stretching, giving the famous pizza pull.
Things that stretch.Glass: Glass is brittle and fractures instead of stretching, although molten glass can be drawn into fibers finer than a hair.
Things that stretch.Brick: Fired clay is hard but brittle, so a brick under strain breaks rather than stretching, which is why walls need mortar and bonding.
Things that stretch.Pencil: A pencil is wood around a graphite core, and it snaps rather than stretches; the core is not lead, though.
Things that stretch.Ceramic mug: Ceramics are very hard but brittle, so a dropped mug shatters instead of bending.
Things that stretch.Wooden spoon: Wood can flex a little, but pull it past that and it splinters; it will never stretch like rubber.
Things that stretch.Coin: A coin is struck between steel dies, and the pressure hardens the metal, so it keeps its shape instead of stretching.
Things that stretch.Cracker: A cracker snaps because baking drives out nearly all moisture, leaving a crisp, brittle structure with no stretch.
Things that stretch.Dry spaghetti: Bend dry spaghetti and it snaps into three or more pieces, a puzzle physicist Richard Feynman famously tried and failed to solve.
Things that stretch.Steel nail: Steel does stretch slightly under load and springs back, but a nail is far too stiff for you to ever see it.
Things that stretch.Chalk: Chalk is soft limestone built from tiny sea creature shells, and it crumbles under force rather than stretching.
Things that stretch.Seashell: A shell is mostly calcium carbonate, the same material as chalk and limestone, so it cracks instead of stretching.
Things that stretch.Marble: Marble is limestone transformed by heat and pressure into a dense, rigid stone that chips and cracks but never stretches.

Things made of cartilage.Outer ear: Springy cartilage gives the outer ear its shape, which is why ears fold over and spring right back.
Things made of cartilage.Nose tip: The tip of the nose is cartilage while the bridge is bone, which is why the tip bends and the bridge does not.
Things made of cartilage.Meniscus: The meniscus cushions the knee, and a torn meniscus is among the commonest knee injuries in athletes.
Things made of cartilage.Epiglottis: The epiglottis is a flap of cartilage that covers the windpipe while you swallow, steering food to the stomach.
Things made of cartilage.Spinal discs: Spinal discs are a ring of fibrous cartilage around a gel center, cushioning the vertebrae and flattening slightly by day.
Things made of cartilage.Shark skeleton: Sharks have no true bones, since their entire skeleton is made of lighter, flexible cartilage.
Things made of cartilage.Tracheal rings: C-shaped rings of cartilage keep the windpipe open so it does not collapse when you breathe in.
Things made of cartilage.Larynx: The larynx is built of cartilage, including the thyroid cartilage that forms the Adam's apple.
Things made of cartilage.Stingray skeleton: Stingrays are relatives of sharks, with skeletons of cartilage, not bone, which keeps them light and flexible.
Things made of cartilage.Femur: A trap: the femur is the longest and strongest bone in the body, made of bone and not cartilage.
Things made of cartilage.Skull: A trap: skull bones fuse together as we grow, though a baby's are separate with soft gaps between them.
Things made of cartilage.Teeth: A trap: tooth enamel is the hardest substance in the body, harder than bone and not at all cartilage.
Things made of cartilage.Kneecap: A trap: the kneecap is bone, though in babies it is still mostly cartilage that hardens over childhood.
Things made of cartilage.Fingernail: A trap: fingernails are keratin, the same protein as hair, and contain no cartilage.
Things made of cartilage.Hair: A trap: hair is made of keratin, a tough protein, and contains no cartilage at all.
Things made of cartilage.Earlobe: A trap: the earlobe is fat and skin with no cartilage, unlike the rest of the ear above it.
Things made of cartilage.Tongue: A trap: the tongue is made of muscle, with no cartilage, which is why it moves so freely.
Things made of cartilage.Collarbone: A trap: the collarbone is bone, and it is one of the most commonly broken bones in the body.
Things made of cartilage.Jawbone: A trap: the jawbone, or mandible, is real bone, and it is the only movable bone of the skull.
Things made of cartilage.Antler: A trap: antlers are bone that deer shed and regrow every year, among the fastest-growing tissues in mammals.
Things made of cartilage.Horse hoof: A trap: hooves are made of keratin, like fingernails, and so contain no cartilage.
Things made of cartilage.Rhino horn: A trap: rhino horn is keratin, like fingernails, not bone or cartilage.
Things made of cartilage.Tusk: A trap: tusks are ivory, which is just elongated teeth, not cartilage.
Things made of cartilage.Toenail: A trap: toenails are keratin, the same protein as fingernails, and contain no cartilage.

Things that have eyes but can't see.Potato: Potato eyes are buds from which new shoots sprout, so a single potato can be cut into pieces that each grow into a new plant.
Things that have eyes but can't see.Needle: The eye of a needle is the hole for thread; in the Bible, it is the famous image for something nearly impossible, a camel passing through.
Things that have eyes but can't see.Hurricane: The calm center of a hurricane is called the eye, usually 30 to 65 kilometers wide, with clear skies surrounded by the fiercest winds.
Things that have eyes but can't see.Peacock feather: The shimmering eyespots on a peacock's train are made by microscopic structures that reflect light, not by pigment, and are used to impress peahens.
Things that have eyes but can't see.Typhoon: Typhoons are the same storm as hurricanes, named for the western Pacific, and like them they have an eye of eerie calm at the center.
Things that have eyes but can't see.Statue: Ancient Greek statues were often given inlaid eyes of glass or stone, which is why some marble figures with blank sockets looked startlingly alive when new.
Things that have eyes but can't see.Doll: Some dolls have eyes that close when laid down, a weighted mechanism that has existed since the 1800s.
Things that have eyes but can't see.Scarecrow: Scarecrows have been used for thousands of years, and ancient Egyptians placed figures in wheat fields to scare quail away from crops.
Things that have eyes but can't see.Snowman: A snowman's eyes are usually pieces of coal or stones, which stare out with no way to see, and they melt away by spring.
Things that have eyes but can't see.Teddy bear: Teddy bears usually have glass or plastic button eyes, and the earliest ones from 1900s Germany used boot buttons.
Things that have eyes but can't see.Mona Lisa: Leonardo's painting is famous for a gaze that seems to follow viewers, and it is painted without eyebrows or lashes, thanks perhaps to fashion or later cleaning.
Things that have eyes but can't see.Garden gnome: Garden gnomes first appeared in Germany in the 1800s, and a gnome's painted eyes watch over many a flower bed.
Things that have eyes but can't see.Spoon: A spoon has a bowl and a handle but no eyes. Only potatoes among everyday foods have eyes, which are the buds that sprout new shoots.
Things that have eyes but can't see.Carrot: A carrot is a taproot, and while a potato has eyes, a carrot has none; it is the snowman's nose, not his eye.
Things that have eyes but can't see.Cloud: A cloud can't see, and only huge storms form an eye, which belongs to the hurricane, not the cloud.
Things that have eyes but can't see.Pillow: A pillow is soft stuffed fabric, so it has no eyes, even though a teddy bear sitting on it would.
Things that have eyes but can't see.Brick: A brick is solid baked clay and has no eyes, though clay bricks often have holes through them in some designs.
Things that have eyes but can't see.Rainbow: A rainbow is sunlight bent through water droplets, so there is nothing in it to look or see.
Things that have eyes but can't see.Thread: Thread goes through the eye of a needle, but it has no eye of its own; it is the thing that passes through.
Things that have eyes but can't see.Lightning: Lightning has no eye, though it can strike inside a hurricane's wall, and a bolt is hotter than the surface of the Sun.
Things that have eyes but can't see.Tree: A tree has knots in its wood, and some people see eyes in them, but they are old branch bases with no sight.
Things that have eyes but can't see.Sock: A sock is a plain tube of fabric with no eyes, until you stick buttons on it to make a puppet.
Things that have eyes but can't see.Volcano: A volcano has a crater, a bowl-shaped mouth at the summit, but no eye; the only eye in the neighborhood belongs to a storm, not a mountain.
Things that have eyes but can't see.Banana: A banana is smooth and has no eyes, unlike a pineapple or potato, whose eyes are scars or buds.

Silly things to wear on a beach day.Snow boots: Heavy snow boots on hot sand would trap sweat. Boots like these are designed to keep feet warm down to well below freezing.
Silly things to wear on a beach day.Ski jacket: A ski jacket is built to hold heat in, so on a hot beach you'd bake. That's the joke, and the reason it sits here.
Silly things to wear on a beach day.Earmuffs: Earmuffs were patented in 1873 by Chester Greenwood, who was only fifteen, because his ears got cold while skating.
Silly things to wear on a beach day.Mittens: Mittens keep fingers together to share warmth, which is why they beat gloves in cold weather and are absurd on sand.
Silly things to wear on a beach day.Wool scarf: Wool is a superb insulator, even when damp, which makes a scarf a hilarious choice on a sunny sandy afternoon.
Silly things to wear on a beach day.Fur coat: A fur coat is built to trap body heat, and animals like arctic foxes keep theirs in temperatures far below zero.
Silly things to wear on a beach day.Ice skates: Ice skates need ice, and a beach has none. Blades on sand make a very slow, very silly kind of walk.
Silly things to wear on a beach day.Snowsuit: A snowsuit is insulation head to toe, so at the beach it works like a sauna, especially in direct sun.
Silly things to wear on a beach day.Balaclava: A balaclava, from the Crimean War town of Balaklava, was knitted to keep soldiers' faces warm in a freezing winter.
Silly things to wear on a beach day.Ski goggles: Ski goggles shield eyes from glare off snow, but they are cut-off from salty air and sun in an odd, comic beach look.
Silly things to wear on a beach day.Thermal underwear: Thermal underwear traps a layer of warm air against the skin, a lifesaver on a mountain, and a sweatbox at the shore.
Silly things to wear on a beach day.Swimsuit: The swimsuit is the obvious beach staple; the first modern ones in the early 1900s still covered most of the body.
Silly things to wear on a beach day.Flip-flops: Flip-flops trace back to ancient Egypt and Rome, and the name imitates the slapping sound of the sole as you walk.
Silly things to wear on a beach day.Sun hat: A sun hat's wide brim can block a good share of the sun's UV from face and neck, a real help on a bright shore.
Silly things to wear on a beach day.Sunglasses: Sunglasses help protect eyes from UV and glare, which bounce off both sand and water on a bright beach day.
Silly things to wear on a beach day.Board shorts: Board shorts got their name from surfers, who wanted a longer, tougher cut that wouldn't chafe against a surfboard.
Silly things to wear on a beach day.Bikini: The bikini was named in 1946 after Bikini Atoll, where atomic tests had just been held, because the designer expected it to be explosive.
Silly things to wear on a beach day.Sarong: A sarong is a wrapped cloth from Southeast Asia, worn for centuries, and is perfect as a beach cover-up or towel.
Silly things to wear on a beach day.Sandals: Sandals may be the oldest footwear: 10,000-year-old ones made of woven fibers were found in a cave in Oregon.
Silly things to wear on a beach day.Rash guard: A rash guard is a stretchy shirt that protects skin from sun and from rubbing against the surfboard.
Silly things to wear on a beach day.Tank top: A tank top is simple summer wear and breathable, so on a beach it's right at home, unlike the winter gear.
Silly things to wear on a beach day.Baseball cap: A baseball cap is a normal beach choice, shading eyes and face; it's an everyday piece of gear, not a joke.
Silly things to wear on a beach day.Cover-up: A cover-up is a light piece worn over a swimsuit on the way to and from the water, so it belongs on the beach.
Silly things to wear on a beach day.Visor: A visor shades the eyes while leaving the head open to the breeze, which is why runners and golfers wear them.

US Navy ranks.Admiral: The top Navy ranks run from one to four stars, with fleet admiral as a five-star wartime rank held by only a few Americans.
US Navy ranks.Ensign: The lowest commissioned Navy officer. A newly graduated officer typically starts here.
US Navy ranks.Commander: Navy commanders often lead ships or squadrons. The rank sits between lieutenant commander and captain.
US Navy ranks.Captain: A Navy captain is a senior officer who commands a large ship, equal to an Army colonel. The Army's captain is far lower.
US Navy ranks.Lieutenant: A Navy lieutenant ranks above lieutenant junior grade, and equals an Army captain. Same word, different weight.
US Navy ranks.Petty Officer: Enlisted sailors who lead others. Their rating badges show a specialty, such as the crossed anchors of a boatswain's mate.
US Navy ranks.Seaman: A junior enlisted sailor. Everyone starting out as a 'seaman recruit' works up through the ranks.
US Navy ranks.Rear Admiral: A flag officer with one or two stars. Its odd name comes from the old fleet divisions: van, centre and rear.
US Navy ranks.Vice Admiral: A three-star Navy rank, found a step above rear admiral. The 'vice' means deputy or substitute.
US Navy ranks.Chief Petty Officer: A senior enlisted sailor, called 'Chief' by everyone. Chiefs are famed for running the Navy's daily operations.
US Navy ranks.Lt. Commander: A mid-level Navy officer, one step beneath commander. The 'lieutenant' part signals a deputy.
US Navy ranks.Colonel: An Army, Air Force and Marine rank, not a Navy one. The Navy equivalent is captain.
US Navy ranks.Major: Army and Marine officers hold this rank, which the Navy lacks. Its equivalent there is lieutenant commander.
US Navy ranks.Sergeant: A rank in the Army, Marines and Air Force, but sailors don't use it. Their nearest equivalent is petty officer.
US Navy ranks.Corporal: An Army and Marine rank. The Navy has no corporals; petty officers fill similar roles.
US Navy ranks.Brigadier: A British Army rank, and the US counterpart is brigadier general. The Navy doesn't use it.
US Navy ranks.Private: An Army and Marine entry grade. Navy sailors start as seaman recruits, so there are no privates afloat.
US Navy ranks.Field Marshal: A top British Army rank, not a Navy one. The naval equivalent is Admiral of the Fleet.
US Navy ranks.Sheriff: A county law officer, not a Navy rank. Sailors have no sheriffs, though ships have masters-at-arms for policing.
US Navy ranks.Constable: A police rank, not a naval one. Though ships have their own security, they call them masters-at-arms.
US Navy ranks.Squire: A medieval knight's attendant. It's a historical term for a noble apprentice, unrelated to the Navy.
US Navy ranks.Deputy: A sheriff's assistant. Naval service has no 'deputy' rank, though it has executive officers as second-in-command.
US Navy ranks.Inspector: A police or inspection rank. It doesn't appear in the US Navy's structure.
US Navy ranks.Baron: A noble title in Europe, not a military rank. It sits below a viscount and above a knight.

Things a carpenter commonly builds.Cabinets: Cabinets are often built with dovetail or dado joints, which let the wood hold firmly with little glue.
Things a carpenter commonly builds.Shelves: A solid shelf can sag over time under books; carpenters add a front lip or a support to keep it level.
Things a carpenter commonly builds.Tables: The oldest wooden tables date back thousands of years, and the Egyptians made them with elegant joints.
Things a carpenter commonly builds.Decks: Carpenters often use pressure-treated lumber for decks, since it resists rot and insects outdoors.
Things a carpenter commonly builds.Staircases: Stairs are among the hardest things to build right, because even a small difference in step height can cause a fall.
Things a carpenter commonly builds.Door frames: Frames must be square and plumb, or the door will stick, and a carpenter checks with a level.
Things a carpenter commonly builds.Wardrobes: The word wardrobe originally meant a room for guarding clothes, and the freestanding wooden cabinet came later.
Things a carpenter commonly builds.Bookcases: Bookcases are not always strong; a shelf loaded with books can carry a large weight if built properly.
Things a carpenter commonly builds.Pergolas: These garden structures made of posts and beams are sometimes covered in climbing plants such as wisteria.
Things a carpenter commonly builds.Benches: A simple bench is one of the oldest pieces of furniture, and carpenters make them for gardens and parks alike.
Things a carpenter commonly builds.Sweaters: A knitter makes sweaters from yarn; the garment's name comes from athletes who wore them to sweat off weight.
Things a carpenter commonly builds.Cakes: A baker makes cakes, and in the world of baking, the use of eggs and sugar goes back to ancient Rome.
Things a carpenter commonly builds.Horseshoes: A farrier or blacksmith forges horseshoes, and the iron shoes are said to bring luck when hung with ends up.
Things a carpenter commonly builds.Candles: A chandler makes candles, and old candles were made from animal fat called tallow, which smelled bad.
Things a carpenter commonly builds.Pottery: A potter shapes clay on a wheel and fires it in a kiln, and the oldest known pottery is about 20,000 years old.
Things a carpenter commonly builds.Jewelry: A jeweler makes it, and ancient shell beads show that people have worn jewelry for over 100,000 years.
Things a carpenter commonly builds.Quilts: Quilters stitch layered fabric, and a patchwork quilt may use thousands of tiny pieces.
Things a carpenter commonly builds.Soap: Soapmakers use fat and lye, and soap-making goes back to ancient Babylon about 4,800 years ago.
Things a carpenter commonly builds.Sausages: A butcher fills casings with minced meat, and sausage-making is a very old art.
Things a carpenter commonly builds.Wedding dresses: A dressmaker creates them, and white weddings were popularized by Queen Victoria in 1840.
Things a carpenter commonly builds.Stained glass: Glaziers cut glass and join it with lead, and medieval cathedrals used it to tell Bible stories to people who couldn't read.
Things a carpenter commonly builds.Wigs: A wigmaker ties each hair by hand, and in the 1700s, wigs were so fashionable that men shaved their heads to wear them.
Things a carpenter commonly builds.Perfume: A perfumer blends scents, and a fine fragrance can contain hundreds of ingredients.
Things a carpenter commonly builds.Neon signs: Glassblowers bend tubes and fill them with gas, and neon gives red-orange, while other gases give other colors.
