Famous internet meme cats.Figaro: Figaro is Geppetto's tuxedo kitten from Disney's Pinocchio, an animated character.

Online ways to say you're laughing.LOL: It started as 'laughing out loud' in 1980s chat, and the Oxford English Dictionary added it in 2011. Today it often just signals friendliness.
Online ways to say you're laughing.ROFL: It stands for 'rolling on the floor laughing', and it's a step beyond LOL from the early internet.
Online ways to say you're laughing.Haha: One of the oldest written laughs, in print for centuries, and the same ha-ha sound turns up in most languages.
Online ways to say you're laughing.Hehe: A quieter, sneakier laugh that suggests mischief, and it has been used in text for decades in online chats.
Online ways to say you're laughing.XD: It's not letters but a face: the X is a squeezed-shut laughing eye and the D is a wide-open mouth, a classic emoticon.
Online ways to say you're laughing.Lulz: A twist on LOL, popularized by the hacking group LulzSec in 2011, meaning laughs at someone else's expense.
Online ways to say you're laughing.Jajaja: Spanish speakers write laughter as 'jajaja' since J sounds like English H, so it's their version of 'hahaha'.
Online ways to say you're laughing.Kek: This laugh began in World of Warcraft, where the Korean 'kekeke' was shown differently in the Horde and Alliance chat languages.
Online ways to say you're laughing.Teehee: A giggle, and it's often used for a cutely mischievous laugh, a wink in text form.
Online ways to say you're laughing.SMH: It stands for 'shaking my head', which signals disbelief or disappointment, so it's a groan rather than a laugh.
Online ways to say you're laughing.BRB: 'Be right back' announces a short absence, and it's been a chat staple since the days of IRC.
Online ways to say you're laughing.IDK: 'I don't know' is a shrug in text form, and it is about as far from laughing as it gets.
Online ways to say you're laughing.TTYL: 'Talk to you later' is a goodbye in text form, not laughter.
Online ways to say you're laughing.AFK: Gamers coined 'away from keyboard' to warn teammates they'd stepped away, which is the opposite of laughing along.
Online ways to say you're laughing.FOMO: 'Fear of missing out' joined the Oxford dictionary in 2013, and it means social anxiety, not laughter.
Online ways to say you're laughing.IMO: 'In my opinion' flags a view, so it can introduce a joke without being one.
Online ways to say you're laughing.TBH: 'To be honest' prefaces a candid remark, and it's more of a confession than a chuckle.
Online ways to say you're laughing.FYI: 'For your information' is office-memo language that long predates the internet, so it's not a laugh.
Online ways to say you're laughing.NVM: 'Never mind' retracts a message, so it's a polite takeback rather than a giggle.
Online ways to say you're laughing.OMG: It expresses shock or excitement, and a 1917 letter to Winston Churchill already used it, long before texting.
Online ways to say you're laughing.IRL: 'In real life' separates the online world from the offline one, so it marks a boundary, not laughter.
Online ways to say you're laughing.BTW: 'By the way' introduces a side remark, so it's a topic change rather than a laugh.
Online ways to say you're laughing.DM: A 'direct message' is a private note, so it's a delivery method, not a laugh.
Online ways to say you're laughing.TIL: 'Today I learned' started on Reddit as a way to share facts, so it brings a smile only if you're lucky.

Apps that come built into an iPhone.Safari: Apple's browser is built on WebKit, itself derived from the KDE project's KHTML engine, and is the only built-in way to browse.
Apps that come built into an iPhone.Camera: Its Live Photo feature records about 1.5 seconds before and after you press the shutter.
Apps that come built into an iPhone.Photos: Uses on-device machine learning to recognize faces, pets and objects so you can search for them.
Apps that come built into an iPhone.Messages: Blue bubbles mean iMessage and green ones mean plain SMS, a color split that has become a social divide.
Apps that come built into an iPhone.FaceTime: Launched with the iPhone 4 in 2010, it brought video calls to a mainstream audience.
Apps that come built into an iPhone.Mail: It handles Gmail accounts, but Gmail itself is a separate app, which is the catch.
Apps that come built into an iPhone.Maps: The 2012 version replaced Google Maps and was so buggy that Tim Cook publicly apologized.
Apps that come built into an iPhone.Weather: Apple's 2020 purchase of Dark Sky helped it deliver those minute-by-minute rain forecasts.
Apps that come built into an iPhone.Clock: Its icon's clock hands move in real time, which is rare for an app icon.
Apps that come built into an iPhone.Calculator: Turn the phone sideways and it becomes a scientific calculator.
Apps that come built into an iPhone.Notes: It can scan documents and sketch with Apple Pencil, so it's more than a text app.
Apps that come built into an iPhone.Wallet: It was called Passbook when it launched in 2012, and it holds cards and boarding passes.
Apps that come built into an iPhone.Health: Launched with iOS 8 in 2014, it counts steps, heart rate and more.
Apps that come built into an iPhone.Gmail: A trap: Google's email app is a download, and it first launched on April 1, 2004, which people thought was a joke.
Apps that come built into an iPhone.Chrome: Google's browser is a separate download, even though iPhones ship with Safari already installed.
Apps that come built into an iPhone.WhatsApp: Meta bought it in 2014 for about $19 billion, and it isn't preinstalled on iPhones.
Apps that come built into an iPhone.Instagram: Facebook bought it for $1 billion in 2012, and it's not preinstalled on iPhones.
Apps that come built into an iPhone.Spotify: A music streaming app you have to download; it launched in 2008 and wasn't ever part of the iPhone's default apps.
Apps that come built into an iPhone.TikTok: Owned by ByteDance, it's a download rather than a built-in iPhone app.
Apps that come built into an iPhone.Uber: Founded as UberCab in 2009, it isn't built into iPhones; you have to download it.
Apps that come built into an iPhone.Google Maps: A trap: iPhones come with Apple Maps, so Google Maps is a download.
Apps that come built into an iPhone.Netflix: Not built in: the iPhone has no streaming TV app of Netflix's kind installed by default; you must download it.
Apps that come built into an iPhone.YouTube: It used to be built in, but Apple removed it in iOS 6 in 2012, so now you have to download it.
Apps that come built into an iPhone.Snapchat: Known for disappearing messages and launched in 2011, it's a download and not preinstalled.

Chess-playing computers and engines.Deep Blue: IBM's computer beat Garry Kasparov in 1997, the first computer to win a match against a reigning world champion.
Chess-playing computers and engines.Stockfish: An open-source engine that has been among the world's strongest for years and is free to use.
Chess-playing computers and engines.AlphaZero: DeepMind's 2017 program that taught itself chess through self-play in about nine hours and crushed Stockfish.
Chess-playing computers and engines.Leela Chess Zero: An open-source engine inspired by AlphaZero, trained by volunteers donating computing power.
Chess-playing computers and engines.Komodo: A strong commercial engine named after the Komodo dragon.
Chess-playing computers and engines.Houdini: An engine from Belgian programmer Robert Houdart that was among the strongest in the early 2010s.
Chess-playing computers and engines.Fritz: A chess software line from ChessBase, and Deep Fritz beat world champion Kramnik in 2006.
Chess-playing computers and engines.Rybka: Vasik Rajlich's engine dominated around 2007 to 2010, but was later stripped of its titles for copying code.
Chess-playing computers and engines.Shredder: Stefan Meyer-Kahlen's engine won multiple world computer chess titles in the 1990s and 2000s.
Chess-playing computers and engines.Watson: A trap: it's IBM's computer that won Jeopardy in 2011, so trivia, not chess.
Chess-playing computers and engines.AlphaGo: A trap: DeepMind's Go program beat Lee Sedol in 2016, but Go isn't chess.
Chess-playing computers and engines.Siri: Apple's voice assistant, not built to play chess like an engine.
Chess-playing computers and engines.Alexa: Amazon's voice assistant, which isn't a chess engine.
Chess-playing computers and engines.ELIZA: A 1960s MIT chatbot that imitated a therapist, so it was never a chess player.
Chess-playing computers and engines.ChatGPT: A language model that can discuss chess but isn't an engine, and it can make illegal moves.
Chess-playing computers and engines.HAL 9000: A trap: it's a fictional computer in 2001: A Space Odyssey, which beats Frank Poole at chess but isn't a real engine.
Chess-playing computers and engines.Skynet: The Terminator's fictional AI, not a real chess engine.
Chess-playing computers and engines.Clippy: Microsoft's old paperclip assistant, which gave Office tips, not chess moves.
Chess-playing computers and engines.Cortana: Microsoft's assistant, named after an AI character in Halo.
Chess-playing computers and engines.Bixby: Samsung's voice assistant, not a chess engine.
Chess-playing computers and engines.Roomba: iRobot's vacuum robot, which cleans floors instead of playing chess.
Chess-playing computers and engines.Furby: A 1998 talking toy, not a chess machine.
Chess-playing computers and engines.Tamagotchi: A 1996 digital pet that lived on a keychain, not a chess machine.
Chess-playing computers and engines.KITT: The talking car from the TV show Knight Rider, a fictional AI, and no chess engine.

Photo editing software.Photoshop: Brothers Thomas and John Knoll created it in 1987, and its name has become a verb for altering any image.
Photo editing software.Lightroom: Adobe's photo organizer and editor works non-destructively, saving your edits as instructions instead of changing the original file.
Photo editing software.GIMP: This free open-source editor, started by two students in 1995, stands for GNU Image Manipulation Program.
Photo editing software.Snapseed: Google's free mobile editor was made by Nik Software, and it uses a swipe-based interface for adjustments.
Photo editing software.Pixelmator: This Mac-focused editor was built by two Lithuanian brothers, and it was Apple's design award winner in 2008.
Photo editing software.Affinity Photo: Serif made it as a one-time-purchase alternative to Adobe's subscriptions, and it is famous for handling huge files smoothly.
Photo editing software.Paint.NET: It began in 2004 as a Washington State University senior project, and it is now a popular free Windows editor.
Photo editing software.VSCO: Its filters mimic classic film stocks, and the app became a style for social photos in the 2010s.
Photo editing software.Photopea: It is a free editor that runs in your browser and opens PSD files, and a single developer in Czechia built it.
Photo editing software.Darktable: This free open-source raw developer is similar to Lightroom, and its name nods to darkroom and table.
Photo editing software.Excel: Microsoft's spreadsheet is used to crunch numbers, and a few artists even make pixel images in cells.
Photo editing software.Word: Its first version arrived in 1983, and it is used for writing, not for editing photos.
Photo editing software.Audacity: This free audio editor, released in 2000, edits sound rather than images.
Photo editing software.GarageBand: Apple's free music studio shipped with Macs from 2004, and it handles sound, not photos.
Photo editing software.Logic Pro: This Apple studio is used for professional music production, so it works with audio rather than images.
Photo editing software.Premiere Pro: Adobe's video editor is behind many films and shows, so it edits video, not stills.
Photo editing software.Final Cut Pro: Apple's editor was used on the Oscar-nominated Cold Mountain, and it handles video.
Photo editing software.Notepad: Microsoft's plain text editor has barely changed since 1983, and it cannot edit images.
Photo editing software.Outlook: This email and calendar program from Microsoft manages messages, not photos.
Photo editing software.Slack: This messaging platform for workplaces was born from a failed video game called Glitch.
Photo editing software.Zoom: Video conferencing exploded from about 10 million daily meeting participants in late 2019 to over 300 million by April 2020.
Photo editing software.Spotify: The streaming service launched in 2008 in Sweden and does music, not photo editing.
Photo editing software.Ableton Live: Made in Berlin, this music tool is built for live performance as well as studio work.
Photo editing software.Pro Tools: Avid's audio workstation has long been a recording studio standard, and it is audio, not images.

Things in the story of Snow White.Poisoned apple: The Evil Queen disguises herself to offer it; in the Grimms' version it's red on one side and white on the other, with only the red half poisoned.
Things in the story of Snow White.Magic mirror: It always tells the truth: the Queen asks who is fairest of all, and when the answer changes, the plot begins.
Things in the story of Snow White.Seven dwarfs: The Grimms left them unnamed; Disney's 1937 film named them Doc, Grumpy, Happy, Sleepy, Bashful, Sneezy and Dopey, and it hasn't left us since.
Things in the story of Snow White.Huntsman: Ordered to kill Snow White, he spares her; in the Grimm version he brings back a boar's lungs and liver as proof for the Queen.
Things in the story of Snow White.Glass coffin: Snow White seems to be dead, so the dwarfs set her in one made of glass; she is revived when it is jolted and the apple dislodges.
Things in the story of Snow White.Evil Queen: Snow White's stepmother, jealous of her beauty; in the first Grimm edition she was her real mother, softened later.
Things in the story of Snow White.Prince: In the Grimms' tale, he comes upon the glass coffin and wants to take it home; his servants' stumble dislodges the apple.
Things in the story of Snow White.Poisoned comb: The Queen's second attempt: she uses a poisoned one to put Snow White to sleep, and the dwarfs remove it in time.
Things in the story of Snow White.Cottage: The dwarfs' small forest home, where Snow White cooks and cleans in exchange for shelter.
Things in the story of Snow White.Glass slipper: It belongs to Cinderella, who loses one at the ball; it's not part of Snow White's story.
Things in the story of Snow White.Pumpkin coach: It belongs to Cinderella, who rides to the ball in one, and does not appear in Snow White.
Things in the story of Snow White.Spinning wheel: The Sleeping Beauty tale uses this tool; Snow White's story has none.
Things in the story of Snow White.Beanstalk: Jack's tale involves a giant at the top; not in Snow White.
Things in the story of Snow White.Fairy Godmother: A Cinderella character who provides the ball dress; not in Snow White.
Things in the story of Snow White.Breadcrumbs: Hansel and Gretel leave a trail of these, but they get eaten; not in Snow White.
Things in the story of Snow White.Red hood: Little Red Riding Hood's cloak is this; it's not in Snow White.
Things in the story of Snow White.Tower: Rapunzel is locked in one; not in Snow White.
Things in the story of Snow White.Frog: A frog features in The Frog Prince, not Snow White.
Things in the story of Snow White.Golden goose: A Grimm tale features a goose with golden feathers; not Snow White.
Things in the story of Snow White.Wolf: Goldilocks samples three bowls of this and finds one just right, so it belongs to a different tale from Snow White's.
Things in the story of Snow White.Porridge: The villain of Little Red Riding Hood and The Three Little Pigs, not Snow White.
Things in the story of Snow White.Pea: The Princess and the Pea is a Hans Christian Andersen tale, where a true princess feels a pea under twenty mattresses.
Things in the story of Snow White.Mermaid: Andersen's Little Mermaid is not in Snow White.
Things in the story of Snow White.Magic lamp: Aladdin's genie lives in one, and not in Snow White.

Best known as playwrights.William Shakespeare: Wrote around 37 plays, and is credited with first recorded uses of hundreds of English words, including 'bedroom' and 'lonely'.
Best known as playwrights.Arthur Miller: Death of a Salesman made him famous in 1949, and The Crucible used the Salem witch trials to criticize McCarthy-era hunts.
Best known as playwrights.Tennessee Williams: Born Thomas Lanier Williams; his A Streetcar Named Desire and The Glass Menagerie defined mid-century American drama.
Best known as playwrights.Henrik Ibsen: The Norwegian whose A Doll's House ended with Nora slamming the door on her marriage, which scandalized 1879 audiences.
Best known as playwrights.Anton Chekhov: Russian dramatist and practising doctor who said medicine was his lawful wife and literature his mistress.
Best known as playwrights.Samuel Beckett: His Waiting for Godot made 'nothing happens, twice' a classic; he won the 1969 Nobel Prize and often wrote first in French.
Best known as playwrights.Molière: Stage name of Jean-Baptiste Poquelin; he collapsed while playing the hypochondriac in his own The Imaginary Invalid and died hours later.
Best known as playwrights.Sophocles: Greek tragedian who wrote over 100 plays, though only seven survive, among them Oedipus Rex and Antigone.
Best known as playwrights.Oscar Wilde: The Importance of Being Earnest, a comedy full of epigrams, is his best-known play; he also wrote one novel.
Best known as playwrights.George Bernard Shaw: The only person to win both a Nobel Prize and an Oscar: Literature in 1925, and for the Pygmalion screenplay in 1938.
Best known as playwrights.Eugene O'Neill: Wrote Long Day's Journey into Night, won four Pulitzer Prizes, and in 1936 became the first American dramatist to win the Nobel.
Best known as playwrights.Harold Pinter: Nobel winner in 2005; his plays are known for ominous silences, so much that a 'Pinter pause' became a term.
Best known as playwrights.Tom Stoppard: Czech-born British writer of Rosencrantz and Guildenstern Are Dead; he also co-wrote the Oscar-winning Shakespeare in Love.
Best known as playwrights.Euripides: Greek tragedian whose Medea and The Bacchae survive; Aristotle called him the most tragic of poets.
Best known as playwrights.Jane Austen: A novelist; her teenage writings did include a few short plays, but her fame rests on novels like Emma.
Best known as playwrights.Emily Dickinson: A poet, not a dramatist; she wrote nearly 1,800 short poems, famous for their dashes and unconventional punctuation.
Best known as playwrights.Herman Melville: A novelist: Moby-Dick is a novel, and Melville's later stories never reached the stage; he died largely forgotten.
Best known as playwrights.J. R. R. Tolkien: A novelist and Oxford professor of languages who wrote The Hobbit and The Lord of the Rings, not a playwright.
Best known as playwrights.Homer: The epic poet behind the Iliad and Odyssey; whether he even existed is debated, and he did not write plays.
Best known as playwrights.Charlotte Brontë: A novelist of Jane Eyre, first published under the male pen name Currer Bell; her sisters Emily and Anne also used pen names.
Best known as playwrights.Walt Whitman: A poet; Leaves of Grass is a book of free verse he revised for most of his life, but he wrote no plays of note.
Best known as playwrights.Mark Twain: A novelist and humorist; he tried writing plays, such as Ah Sin, but they flopped, and his fame stayed with Tom Sawyer.
Best known as playwrights.Vincent van Gogh: A painter who sold very little in his lifetime and produced about 2,000 artworks in roughly a decade; no plays.
Best known as playwrights.Claude Monet: A painter whose Impression, Sunrise gave Impressionism its name after a critic mocked the title in 1874; not a dramatist.

Fictional detectives from books.Sherlock Holmes: Modeled by Arthur Conan Doyle on Dr. Joseph Bell; he never says 'Elementary, my dear Watson' in the original stories.
Fictional detectives from books.Hercule Poirot: The Belgian egotist; when Christie killed him in Curtain, the New York Times ran a front-page obituary in 1975.
Fictional detectives from books.Miss Marple: The spinster of St Mary Mead solves crimes by comparing them to village gossip, first appearing in 1927.
Fictional detectives from books.Nancy Drew: Created in 1930 and written by many ghostwriters under the name Carolyn Keene; she has appeared in over 175 books.
Fictional detectives from books.Philip Marlowe: Raymond Chandler's wisecracking Los Angeles private eye, debuted in The Big Sleep in 1939.
Fictional detectives from books.Sam Spade: Dashiell Hammett's San Francisco private eye of The Maltese Falcon, played by Bogart in 1941.
Fictional detectives from books.Inspector Morse: Colin Dexter's Oxford detective, whose first name, Endeavour, he hides for much of the series.
Fictional detectives from books.Father Brown: G. K. Chesterton's priest sleuth, who solves crimes by understanding human nature and sin rather than by clues.
Fictional detectives from books.Lord Peter Wimsey: Dorothy L. Sayers's aristocratic sleuth, a monocled collector of rare books who debuted in 1923.
Fictional detectives from books.Auguste Dupin: Poe's 1841 Murders in the Rue Morgue introduced him, in what is widely regarded as the first detective story.
Fictional detectives from books.Jules Maigret: Georges Simenon's Paris police commissaire, hero of 75 novels, who solves cases by absorbing the atmosphere.
Fictional detectives from books.Encyclopedia Brown: Donald J. Sobol's boy detective of Idaville, who solved cases from 1963 and offered readers solutions in the back.
Fictional detectives from books.Professor Moriarty: Holmes's arch-nemesis, not a detective; he appears in only two of the original stories.
Fictional detectives from books.Arsène Lupin: Maurice Leblanc's gentleman thief, who once even outwits a Sherlock look-alike; a crook, not a detective.
Fictional detectives from books.Raffles: E. W. Hornung's gentleman burglar, created by Conan Doyle's brother-in-law as a Holmes reverse.
Fictional detectives from books.Fagin: Dickens's pickpocket boss in Oliver Twist, a crook rather than a detective, with a gang of boys.
Fictional detectives from books.Dracula: Stoker's vampire count, hunted by Van Helsing; a villain, not a detective.
Fictional detectives from books.Long John Silver: Stevenson's one-legged pirate with a parrot, who helped define the pirate image; a rogue, not a detective.
Fictional detectives from books.Captain Nemo: Verne's submarine captain, whose name is Latin for 'no one'; an inventor, not a detective.
Fictional detectives from books.Phileas Fogg: Verne's traveler who bets £20,000 he can circle the globe in 80 days; he's an adventurer, not a detective.
Fictional detectives from books.Tom Ripley: Patricia Highsmith's charming murderer, a con man who gets away with it; a villain, not a detective.
Fictional detectives from books.Hannibal Lecter: A cannibal psychiatrist who helps the FBI but is a killer, not a detective.
Fictional detectives from books.Jay Gatsby: Fitzgerald's mysterious millionaire, throwing lavish parties to win back Daisy, but never solving crimes.
Fictional detectives from books.Atticus Finch: A lawyer, not a detective, defending Tom Robinson in To Kill a Mockingbird, with a quiet moral courage.

Characters in Charlie and the Chocolate.Willy Wonka: Willy Wonka's factory was inspired by Dahl's schooldays, when Cadbury sent chocolates to his school to be taste-tested.
Characters in Charlie and the Chocolate.Charlie Bucket: Charlie Bucket is the poor boy who wins a Golden Ticket and lives with four grandparents in one small house.
Characters in Charlie and the Chocolate.Grandpa Joe: Grandpa Joe has been bedridden for twenty years when he leaps out of bed to join the tour in the story.
Characters in Charlie and the Chocolate.Augustus Gloop: Augustus Gloop is the greedy boy who falls into the chocolate river and is sucked up a pipe.
Characters in Charlie and the Chocolate.Veruca Salt: Veruca Salt is the spoiled girl who tries to grab a squirrel and gets thrown down the garbage chute.
Characters in Charlie and the Chocolate.Violet Beauregarde: Violet Beauregarde is the gum-chewer who turns into a giant blueberry after testing an experimental gum.
Characters in Charlie and the Chocolate.Mike Teavee: Mike Teavee is the TV-obsessed boy who is shrunk when he gets sent through the air by television.
Characters in Charlie and the Chocolate.Oompa-Loompas: The Oompa-Loompas, from Loompaland, work for Wonka for cocoa beans and sing moralizing songs about each naughty child.
Characters in Charlie and the Chocolate.Grandma Josephine: Grandma Josephine is one of Charlie's four grandparents, who share one bed in a tiny house.
Characters in Charlie and the Chocolate.Mr. Salt: Mr. Salt, Veruca's father, owns a peanut factory and his workers shell nuts to find a Golden Ticket.
Characters in Charlie and the Chocolate.Matilda: Matilda is a Dahl heroine, not from the chocolate factory, with telekinetic powers and a love of books.
Characters in Charlie and the Chocolate.Miss Trunchbull: Miss Trunchbull is the awful headmistress in Matilda, not in Charlie and the Chocolate Factory.
Characters in Charlie and the Chocolate.Miss Honey: Miss Honey is Matilda's gentle teacher in Matilda, and the cruel headmistress Trunchbull is actually her aunt.
Characters in Charlie and the Chocolate.The BFG: The BFG is the giant who blows dreams into children's bedrooms, and he speaks his own language of snozzcumbers and whizzpopping.
Characters in Charlie and the Chocolate.Sophie: Sophie is the orphan the BFG snatches, and Dahl named her after his granddaughter.
Characters in Charlie and the Chocolate.Mr. Fox: Mr. Fox is the hero of Fantastic Mr Fox, who digs a tunnel to steal from three mean farmers.
Characters in Charlie and the Chocolate.Mr. Twit: Mr. Twit has a beard where old food gets stuck; he and Mrs Twit play nasty tricks in The Twits.
Characters in Charlie and the Chocolate.Bruce Bogtrotter: Bruce Bogtrotter is the boy forced to eat a giant chocolate cake in Matilda, which is a different book.
Characters in Charlie and the Chocolate.Grand High Witch: The Grand High Witch is the villain of Dahl's The Witches, not Charlie and the Chocolate Factory.
Characters in Charlie and the Chocolate.Aunt Sponge: Aunt Sponge is flattened by the Giant Peach in James and the Giant Peach, freeing James to escape.
Characters in Charlie and the Chocolate.Aunt Spiker: Aunt Spiker is the thin, nasty aunt in James and the Giant Peach, and she is flattened with her sister.
Characters in Charlie and the Chocolate.Mrs. Wormwood: Mrs. Wormwood is Matilda's neglectful mother, who loves bingo and television more than her child.
Characters in Charlie and the Chocolate.Boggis: Boggis is the chicken farmer in Fantastic Mr Fox, one of three mean farmers.
Characters in Charlie and the Chocolate.Bunce: Bunce is the short duck-and-goose farmer in Fantastic Mr Fox, who eats doughnuts stuffed with goose liver.

Words coined in literature.Robot: Karel Čapek's 1920 play R.U.R. coined it from Czech robota, "forced labor"; his brother Josef suggested the word.
Words coined in literature.Scrooge: Dickens named him in A Christmas Carol (1843); "scrooge" now means any miser, and "Bah! Humbug" is his catchphrase.
Words coined in literature.Chortle: Lewis Carroll coined it in "Jabberwocky" (1871) as a blend of "chuckle" and "snort".
Words coined in literature.Utopia: Thomas More's 1516 book coined it from Greek, a pun on "no place" and "good place".
Words coined in literature.Cyberspace: William Gibson coined it in his 1982 short story "Burning Chrome" and made it famous in Neuromancer (1984).
Words coined in literature.Pandemonium: Milton named Satan's capital this in Paradise Lost (1667), from Greek for "all demons".
Words coined in literature.Tintinnabulation: Poe popularised it in "The Bells" ("the tintinnabulation that so musically wells"), from Latin tintinnabulum, "little bell".
Words coined in literature.Catch-22: Joseph Heller's 1961 novel turned it into a term for a no-win, self-contradictory trap; his working title had been Catch-18.
Words coined in literature.Yahoo: Swift's Gulliver's Travels (1726) used it for brutish humanlike creatures; the web company chose it, joking they were yahoos.
Words coined in literature.Lilliputian: Gulliver's tiny hosts in Swift's 1726 satire stood about six inches tall, so the adjective now means very small.
Words coined in literature.Galumph: Another "Jabberwocky" coinage by Carroll, a blend of "gallop" and "triumph" meaning to move heavily.
Words coined in literature.Quark: Physicist Murray Gell-Mann borrowed it from Finnegans Wake ("Three quarks for Muster Mark!") for subatomic particles.
Words coined in literature.Grok: Robert Heinlein's Stranger in a Strange Land (1961) coined it for understanding something so fully that you merge with it.
Words coined in literature.Doublethink: Orwell's Nineteen Eighty-Four (1949) coined it for holding two contradictory beliefs at once and accepting both.
Words coined in literature.Television: Constantin Perskyi coined it at the 1900 Paris World's Fair, in a scientific paper rather than a story.
Words coined in literature.Algebra: It comes from Arabic al-jabr via the mathematician al-Khwarizmi, in a scientific treatise, not literature.
Words coined in literature.Banana: English borrowed it from a West African language through Spanish and Portuguese traders.
Words coined in literature.Shampoo: From Hindi champo, "to massage", brought by the British from India in the 1700s.
Words coined in literature.Ketchup: From a Chinese word, probably Hokkien ke-tsiap, a fish sauce, meaning ketchup's origin isn't literary at all.
Words coined in literature.Pizza: Pizza appears in a Latin document from Gaeta, Italy, dated 997, long before any author coined it for fiction.
Words coined in literature.Laser: An acronym for "light amplification by stimulated emission of radiation" made up by physicist Gordon Gould in 1957.
Words coined in literature.Radar: The US Navy coined this acronym in 1940: "radio detection and ranging".
Words coined in literature.Sandwich: John Montagu, the fourth Earl of Sandwich, gave it his name in the 1700s, so it's an eponym, not a literary coinage.
Words coined in literature.Boycott: Named for Captain Charles Boycott, an estate agent shunned by neighbors in Ireland in 1880; a real event, not fiction.

Printmaking techniques.Etching: Acid bites lines into a metal plate; Rembrandt's etchings made him one of history's great printmakers.
Printmaking techniques.Woodcut: The oldest printmaking method, it's behind Japanese ukiyo-e, including Hokusai's Great Wave.
Printmaking techniques.Lithography: Alois Senefelder invented it in 1796; it works because oil and water repel each other on a flat stone.
Printmaking techniques.Screen printing: Andy Warhol's Marilyn and soup can prints popularized it as art; ink is forced through a mesh stencil.
Printmaking techniques.Engraving: A sharp burin cuts lines into metal; banknotes are still engraved so counterfeits are hard to copy.
Printmaking techniques.Linocut: Carved into a block of linoleum, it was used by Picasso for bold posters in the 1950s.
Printmaking techniques.Monotype: Each print is unique, because the painted image is transferred to paper once and can't be repeated exactly.
Printmaking techniques.Aquatint: Goya used it for tonal washes in his Disasters of War, by acid biting through powdered resin.
Printmaking techniques.Drypoint: A needle scratches directly into the plate, leaving a burr of metal that gives lines a velvety look; Rembrandt used it.
Printmaking techniques.Mezzotint: The plate is roughened all over with a rocker, so it prints solid black and the artist burnishes the lights; it dates from the 1640s.
Printmaking techniques.Fresco: Fresco paints pigment into wet plaster, so it's painting, not printmaking; Michelangelo's Sistine ceiling is one.
Printmaking techniques.Tempera: Tempera uses egg yolk as a binder for painting, a medieval technique, not printing.
Printmaking techniques.Impasto: Impasto is paint laid on thickly, as Van Gogh did; it's a painting texture.
Printmaking techniques.Sfumato: Sfumato is Leonardo's smoky softening of edges in paint, as in the Mona Lisa.
Printmaking techniques.Mosaic: A mosaic is built from small pieces called tesserae, so it's an assembled picture, not a printed one.
Printmaking techniques.Collage: Collage means "gluing" in French; Picasso and Braque began pasting paper into art around 1912.
Printmaking techniques.Origami: Origami is Japanese paper folding, a craft of folds rather than printed ink.
Printmaking techniques.Batik: Batik is a wax-resist dyeing craft from Indonesia, recognized by UNESCO in 2009.
Printmaking techniques.Embroidery: Embroidery is stitched thread; the Bayeux Tapestry is actually an embroidery, not a tapestry.
Printmaking techniques.Calligraphy: Calligraphy is decorative writing by hand, not a printing process.
Printmaking techniques.Pottery: Pottery is shaped and fired clay, among the oldest crafts, so it's not printmaking.
Printmaking techniques.Quilting: Quilting stitches layers of fabric, so it's textile craft instead of printmaking.
Printmaking techniques.Weaving: Weaving interlaces threads on a loom, so it's textile work and not printmaking.
Printmaking techniques.Glassblowing: Glassblowing was invented around the first century BC, probably in the Roman Near East, and shapes molten glass.

Fictional pirates.Captain Hook: Barrie's pirate is James Hook, who fears the crocodile that swallowed his hand and a ticking clock.
Fictional pirates.Long John Silver: Stevenson's one-legged cook invented much of what we imagine as a pirate, including the parrot on the shoulder.
Fictional pirates.Smee: Hook's cheerful, spectacled boatswain is more silly than sinister, a fussy tailor-like pirate who loves his captain.
Fictional pirates.Dread Pirate Roberts: The title in The Princess Bride is passed from one man to the next, so Westley is not the first Dread Pirate Roberts.
Fictional pirates.Captain Flint: Silver's parrot is named for this dead captain and squawks 'Pieces of eight!', while Flint himself is long dead.
Fictional pirates.Israel Hands: A real Israel Hands was Blackbeard's gunner, and Stevenson borrowed the name for this Treasure Island mutineer.
Fictional pirates.Black Dog: This is the first pirate to track Billy Bones to the Admiral Benbow inn, setting Jim Hawkins off on his adventure.
Fictional pirates.Blind Pew: The blind pirate delivers the Black Spot and taps his stick down the road, until horses run him down.
Fictional pirates.Billy Bones: The old seaman's chest holds the treasure map, and he sings 'Fifteen men on the dead man's chest', a line Stevenson invented.
Fictional pirates.Captain Pugwash: The cartoon pirate's rude crew names are an urban myth; his creator John Ryan denied them.
Fictional pirates.Red Rackham: The pirate in Tintin's The Secret of the Unicorn is named after real buccaneer Calico Jack Rackham, and Haddock's ancestor defeated him.
Fictional pirates.Captain Blood: Rafael Sabatini's 1922 hero is an Irish doctor turned pirate, played by Errol Flynn in the 1935 film.
Fictional pirates.Captain Ahab: Melville's captain hunts the white whale Moby-Dick, not ships, and he commands a whaler, so he is no pirate.
Fictional pirates.Captain Haddock: Haddock is a merchant captain, not a pirate, but his ancestor Sir Francis Haddock fought the pirate Red Rackham.
Fictional pirates.Captain Smollett: Smollett is the honest ship's captain who opposes the pirates, named after novelist Tobias Smollett.
Fictional pirates.Captain Bligh: Bligh faced a mutiny on the Bounty in 1789, so he was the victim of rebels, not a pirate himself.
Fictional pirates.Horatio Hornblower: C. S. Forester's Royal Navy officer, said to inspire Star Trek's Kirk, fights pirates rather than being one.
Fictional pirates.Jack Aubrey: Patrick O'Brian's Royal Navy captain, played by Russell Crowe, is a naval hero, not a pirate.
Fictional pirates.Ishmael: Ishmael is the narrator who survives Moby-Dick's sinking, beginning 'Call me Ishmael', and is a sailor, not a pirate.
Fictional pirates.Queequeg: The tattooed South Sea harpooneer in Moby-Dick is Ishmael's friend, and he works on a whaler, not a pirate ship.
Fictional pirates.Gulliver: In Swift's tale Gulliver is attacked by pirates, but he is a ship's surgeon, not a pirate.
Fictional pirates.Robinson Crusoe: Defoe's castaway is captured by Salé pirates early in the novel and enslaved, so he's a victim here.
Fictional pirates.Sinbad: Sinbad of the Arabian Nights sails as a merchant, meeting giant birds and sea monsters, and never robs ships.
Fictional pirates.Popeye: Segar's spinach-eating sailor, who debuted in 1929, fights Bluto but is a sailor rather than a pirate.

Slimy things.Slug: A slug's slime lets it glide over a razor blade unharmed, and some species follow their own trail back home.
Slimy things.Snail: Snail slime does two jobs: it's sticky enough to grip, then thins out as the foot moves, so one secretion handles grip and glide.
Slimy things.Slime: Brainless slime molds can solve mazes, growing toward food along the shortest route and ignoring dead ends.
Slimy things.Eel: An eel's slime coat helps it wriggle through tight spaces and guards against parasites and abrasion.
Slimy things.Earthworm: Earthworms breathe through their moist, mucus-coated skin, which is why so many surface when heavy rain floods their burrows.
Slimy things.Hagfish: Threatened, a hagfish can turn a bucket of seawater into slime in seconds; despite the nickname slime eel, it isn't an eel.
Slimy things.Snot: Your nose and sinuses make about a liter of mucus a day, and you swallow nearly all of it without noticing.
Slimy things.Okra: Okra's gooey sap is what thickens gumbo, and the dish's name likely comes from a West African word for okra.
Slimy things.Frogspawn: Frogspawn's jelly swells in water to cushion the eggs, and its dark yolks soak up sunlight to warm the developing tadpoles.
Slimy things.Snake: Snakes only look slimy; their scaly skin is dry and smooth, and many people are surprised the first time they touch one.
Slimy things.Lizard: Lizard skin is dry and scaly, so the slimy-reptile idea is a myth; truly moist skin belongs to amphibians.
Slimy things.Toad: Toads are the sneaky trap: their warty skin is drier than a frog's, and the warts won't give you warts.
Slimy things.Cactus: Cactus stems store a gooey gel inside, but the waxy, spiny outside feels dry, so it isn't slimy to the touch.
Slimy things.Sandpaper: The grit on sandpaper is often aluminum oxide or garnet, hard crushed minerals that make it about as unslimy as it gets.
Slimy things.Cracker: Crackers are baked dry so they stay crisp for months, and moisture is their enemy, which makes them the opposite of slimy.
Slimy things.Feather: Birds spread oil from a gland near the tail across their feathers while preening, keeping them water-repellent rather than slimy.
Slimy things.Pebble: Pebbles feel slick when polished by water, but they only turn slimy when a film of algae grows on them.
Slimy things.Sand: Most beach sand is ground-down quartz, which is why it sparkles under a magnifying glass; dry sand is anything but slimy.
Slimy things.Leather: Leather is animal skin tanned so it won't rot, and the process turns a soft, wet hide into something dry and supple.
Slimy things.Turtle shell: A turtle's shell is part of its skeleton, fused to its ribs and spine, and its surface is hard and dry.
Slimy things.Pinecone: Pinecones close in damp weather and open when it's dry, so their scales act as a tiny natural forecaster.
Slimy things.Tortilla chip: Tortilla chips come from corn soaked in limewater, an ancient process called nixtamalization that also boosts the corn's nutrition.
Slimy things.Wool sweater: Wool fibers have microscopic scales that lock together when agitated, which is how one hot wash can shrink a sweater to doll size.
Slimy things.Tree bark: Bark is a tree's dry armor; cork oaks are special because their bark can be stripped for wine stoppers without killing the tree.

Alloys (metals mixed from others).Steel: Steel is iron plus a little carbon, and the Bessemer process of the 1850s made it cheap enough to build cities with.
Alloys (metals mixed from others).Brass: Brass is copper and zinc, and its golden shine is why it's used for instruments and doorknobs.
Alloys (metals mixed from others).Bronze: Bronze is copper mixed with tin, and it gave its name to the Bronze Age.
Alloys (metals mixed from others).Pewter: Pewter is mostly tin with antimony and copper, and modern versions are lead-free.
Alloys (metals mixed from others).Sterling silver: Sterling silver is 92.5 percent silver, usually blended with copper for strength.
Alloys (metals mixed from others).Solder: Traditional solder is tin and lead, while modern plumbing solder is lead-free.
Alloys (metals mixed from others).Stainless steel: Stainless steel needs at least about 10.5 percent chromium, which forms an invisible protective layer.
Alloys (metals mixed from others).White gold: White gold is gold alloyed with white metals like palladium or nickel and often plated with rhodium.
Alloys (metals mixed from others).Rose gold: Rose gold's pink hue comes from mixing gold with copper.
Alloys (metals mixed from others).Copper: Copper is a pure element; mix it with tin or zinc and you get bronze or brass.
Alloys (metals mixed from others).Iron: Pure iron is soft and seldom used, and steel is its alloy.
Alloys (metals mixed from others).Tin: Pure tin is an element, and bending a bar of it produces a creak called tin cry.
Alloys (metals mixed from others).Zinc: Zinc is an element, and with copper it makes brass.
Alloys (metals mixed from others).Aluminum: Aluminum is an element, though most everyday aluminum items, from cans to airplane parts, are alloys.
Alloys (metals mixed from others).Platinum: Platinum is an element; jewelry labeled platinum is usually 90 to 95 percent pure.
Alloys (metals mixed from others).Lead: Lead is a pure element, dense and soft enough to scratch with a fingernail.
Alloys (metals mixed from others).Nickel: Nickel is an element, and the US nickel coin is an alloy that's mostly copper.
Alloys (metals mixed from others).Titanium: Titanium is an element, though aerospace uses alloys with aluminum and vanadium.
Alloys (metals mixed from others).Mercury: Mercury is a pure element; when it combines with other metals the result is called an amalgam.
Alloys (metals mixed from others).Tungsten: Tungsten has the highest melting point of any metal, about 3,400 degrees Celsius.
Alloys (metals mixed from others).24-karat gold: 24-karat means pure gold; any lower karat number means it's alloyed.
Alloys (metals mixed from others).Chromium: Chromium is an element that gives stainless steel and chrome plating their shine.
Alloys (metals mixed from others).Cobalt: Cobalt is an element that gives glass and pottery a deep blue, called cobalt blue.
Alloys (metals mixed from others).Magnesium: Magnesium is an element that burns with a brilliant white flame, as in old camera flashes.

Things designed to be waterproof.Rain boots: Rain boots are often called Wellingtons after the Duke of Wellington, who favored a style of boot in the early 1800s.
Things designed to be waterproof.Umbrella: Umbrellas began as sunshades in ancient Egypt, China and Mesopotamia, and the word comes from Latin umbra, shadow.
Things designed to be waterproof.Raincoat: Charles Macintosh patented rubberized fabric in 1824, and Brits still call raincoats macs.
Things designed to be waterproof.Wetsuit: Neoprene is full of tiny gas bubbles that insulate, and a thin layer of water trapped inside warms to body temperature.
Things designed to be waterproof.Tarp: Tarp is short for tarpaulin, from tar and pall, because sailors waterproofed canvas with tar.
Things designed to be waterproof.Diving watch: A Rolex experimental watch was strapped to James Cameron's submersible that reached the Mariana Trench in 2012.
Things designed to be waterproof.Shower curtain: Shower curtains billow inward, and physicists still argue over exactly why.
Things designed to be waterproof.Swim goggles: Swim goggles are sealed with silicone gaskets, and ancient Persian pearl divers reportedly used polished tortoiseshell.
Things designed to be waterproof.Fishing waders: Breathable waders use fabric with pores small enough to block liquid water yet release sweat vapor.
Things designed to be waterproof.Poncho: The poncho is a South American garment, a single piece of cloth with a hole for the head.
Things designed to be waterproof.Dry bag: Rolling a dry bag's top a few times makes a watertight seal.
Things designed to be waterproof.Kayak: Kayak means hunter's boat in the Inuit language, and the original ones were sealskin stretched over frames.
Things designed to be waterproof.Sponge: A sponge is a living animal, and natural ones are the skeletons of sea creatures.
Things designed to be waterproof.Paper towel: Paper towels were invented in 1907 by Scott Paper after a batch of toilet paper turned out too thick.
Things designed to be waterproof.Cotton T-shirt: Cotton absorbs a lot of water and dries slowly, which is why hikers say cotton kills.
Things designed to be waterproof.Bath towel: Terry loops in a towel give water far more surface to cling to than flat fabric would.
Things designed to be waterproof.Cardboard box: Corrugated cardboard loses strength when damp, so boxes crumple in the rain.
Things designed to be waterproof.Wool sock: Wool can absorb nearly a third of its weight in moisture and still feel dry.
Things designed to be waterproof.Paper bag: Margaret Knight invented the flat-bottomed paper bag in 1871.
Things designed to be waterproof.Tissue: Kleenex was first marketed in 1924 as a way to remove cold cream.
Things designed to be waterproof.Sugar cube: Sugar dissolves in water, so a sugar cube is a poor choice for a rainy day.
Things designed to be waterproof.Canvas sneakers: Canvas was waxed to make sailcloth and tents water-resistant, but plain canvas soaks through.
Things designed to be waterproof.Denim jeans: Denim's name comes from serge de Nimes, a French fabric, and wet jeans take ages to dry.
Things designed to be waterproof.Mop: Mops work because their many tiny fibers hold water between them as well as in them.

Wrinkly things.Raisin: A raisin is a dried grape; it wrinkles as water leaves, and a grape can shrink to about a quarter of its weight.
Wrinkly things.Prune: Prunes are dried European plums, and their name became so unfashionable that California producers rebranded them 'dried plums'.
Wrinkly things.Shar-Pei: This Chinese breed's deep folds were bred for fighting dogs, giving an opponent a loose hide that was hard to grip.
Wrinkly things.Walnut: A walnut kernel's folded lobes look strikingly like a brain, which medieval herbalists took as a sign it was good for the mind.
Wrinkly things.Brain: The human brain's folds let a large cortex fit inside the skull; flattened out, it would cover about a pillowcase.
Wrinkly things.Pug: Pugs have deep facial wrinkles that need regular cleaning, and the breed was favored by Chinese emperors centuries ago.
Wrinkly things.Crumpled paper: Crumpled paper is surprisingly strong and resists further crushing, which is why physicists study it as a model of stress.
Wrinkly things.Bathtub fingers: Pruney fingers aren't just waterlogging: nerves trigger blood vessels to constrict, and the ridges may improve grip on wet objects.
Wrinkly things.Naked mole rat: These hairless East African rodents live over 30 years, resist cancer and feel little pain from acid, all with famously wrinkled skin.
Wrinkly things.Elephant skin: An elephant's wrinkles trap water and mud, which helps it stay cool and keeps its skin from drying out.
Wrinkly things.Sun-dried tomato: Sun-dried tomatoes lose most of their water as they dry, concentrating flavor, and are often preserved in oil.
Wrinkly things.Savoy cabbage: Savoy cabbage has crinkled, lacy leaves unlike smooth green cabbage, and its texture holds sauces well.
Wrinkly things.Grape: A grape is smooth and plump with taut skin; it only turns wrinkly after drying into a raisin.
Wrinkly things.Plum: A fresh plum is smooth with a dusty bloom, and it only wrinkles when dried into a prune.
Wrinkly things.Balloon: A balloon is stretched smooth by the air inside, and it only wrinkles when it deflates.
Wrinkly things.Marble: A marble is polished to be perfectly smooth, which is why it rolls so predictably.
Wrinkly things.Mirror: A mirror is deliberately flat, and even tiny ripples in the glass would warp every reflection.
Wrinkly things.Bowling ball: A bowling ball's surface is smooth and polished, apart from the finger holes, with a dense core that affects its roll.
Wrinkly things.Egg: An eggshell looks smooth but is covered in thousands of tiny pores that let the embryo breathe.
Wrinkly things.Ice cube: An ice cube is smooth when frozen, though bubbles trapped inside often make it cloudy rather than clear.
Wrinkly things.Banana: A banana peel is smooth until it ripens and spots up; the fruit itself isn't wrinkled at all.
Wrinkly things.Apple: A fresh apple has taut, waxy skin that wrinkles only after long storage as it loses moisture.
Wrinkly things.Cherry: A cherry is glossy and smooth, and only wrinkles when dried, as in the cherries used in trail mixes.
Wrinkly things.Tomato: A fresh tomato is smooth and tight-skinned; a wrinkled one has simply lost water and gone soft.

Things on a city street.Lamppost: Early street lamps burned oil or gas and were lit by lamplighters each evening, who walked around with poles at dusk and dawn.
Things on a city street.Fire hydrant: Hydrants are typically painted bright colors and kept clear of parked cars, and many US cities fine drivers who block one.
Things on a city street.Crosswalk: The zebra crossing first appeared in Britain in 1951, and its black-and-white stripes were named for the animal's pattern.
Things on a city street.Traffic light: The first electric traffic light appeared in Cleveland in 1914, and the earlier 1868 London version was a gas lantern that exploded.
Things on a city street.Manhole: Manhole covers are round because a circular lid can never fall through its own opening, however you turn it.
Things on a city street.Parking meter: The first parking meter was installed in Oklahoma City in 1935, and its inventor wanted to stop downtown workers from hogging the spaces.
Things on a city street.Bus stop: Many cities now use real-time displays at stops, which show predicted arrivals taken from GPS signals on the buses themselves.
Things on a city street.Curb: Curbs funnel rainwater to the drains, and the dropped section at corners, called a curb cut, helps wheelchair users and strollers alike.
Things on a city street.Mailbox: Pillar boxes in Britain date to the 1850s, and the novelist Anthony Trollope, a post office official, helped introduce them.
Things on a city street.Bench: Many city benches are designed with armrests in the middle or sloped seats to discourage sleeping, a style critics call hostile architecture.
Things on a city street.Bike lane: Copenhagen and Amsterdam are famed for bike lanes, and in Copenhagen more than a third of commutes are made by bicycle.
Things on a city street.Storm drain: Storm drains usually lead untreated to rivers or the sea, which is why you shouldn't pour anything harmful down them.
Things on a city street.Newsstand: Newsstands once sold the day's papers to commuters, and in New York many still sell magazines, candy and subway cards.
Things on a city street.Haystack: Haystacks stand in fields, and Claude Monet painted a famous series of them in different light, which hung in cities but not on streets.
Things on a city street.Igloo: Igloos are Arctic snow houses, and the inside can reach well above freezing from body heat alone, though not in a city street.
Things on a city street.Stalactite: Stalactites hang in caves and grow incredibly slowly, often just a few centimeters in a century, so you won't see them in a city.
Things on a city street.Silo: Silos store grain on farms, and the tall cylinders are sealed to keep the contents dry; they are not common on busy streets.
Things on a city street.Tumbleweed: Tumbleweeds are dried plants that roll across deserts, and the plant known in the American West actually came from Russia.
Things on a city street.Coral reef: Coral reefs cover less than one percent of the ocean floor but host roughly a quarter of marine species, far from any street.
Things on a city street.Glacier: Glaciers are slow rivers of ice that flow under their own weight, found in mountains and polar regions rather than on a street corner.
Things on a city street.Sand dune: Dunes shift with the wind, and some desert ones, like those of the Sahara, can slowly migrate several meters in a year.
Things on a city street.Termite mound: Some termite mounds in Africa and Australia rise several meters, and their ventilation channels keep the colony's temperature steady.
Things on a city street.Paddy field: Paddy fields are flooded plots where rice grows, and rice feeds more than half the world, but they belong to countryside, not city streets.
Things on a city street.Geyser: Geysers like Old Faithful erupt from superheated water underground, which isn't a city street fixture despite a burst hydrant's resemblance.

Hats with a brim.Fedora: The fedora is named after Victorien Sardou's 1882 play Fédora, in which the heroine wore one. Humphrey Bogart made it a film noir classic.
Hats with a brim.Sombrero: A sombrero's wide brim shades the wearer from the Mexican sun, which is where it gets its name, from Spanish 'sombra'.
Hats with a brim.Cowboy hat: The Stetson, designed by John B. Stetson in 1865, was nicknamed the 'ten-gallon hat' though it can't hold anywhere near that.
Hats with a brim.Panama hat: Panama hats are woven from toquilla straw in Ecuador, not Panama. The name stuck when they were shipped from Panama and worn by canal workers.
Hats with a brim.Bowler: The bowler was designed in 1849 by London hatmakers Lock & Co. for a gamekeeper who needed a hard hat against low branches.
Hats with a brim.Trilby: The trilby is named for George du Maurier's 1894 novel Trilby, whose stage adaptation featured the hat. It has a shorter brim than the fedora.
Hats with a brim.Boater: The flat-topped straw boater was once worn by gondoliers and rowers. Maurice Chevalier made it his trademark.
Hats with a brim.Top hat: Top hats were the standard in Victorian formal dress. Silk versions were so tall that Abraham Lincoln famously used his as a filing cabinet.
Hats with a brim.Sun hat: The sun hat's wide brim blocks UV rays that burn the face and neck. Straw ones are cool because they let air circulate.
Hats with a brim.Bucket hat: Bucket hats began as Irish fishermen's hats in the early 1900s. They became street style in the 1980s through hip-hop.
Hats with a brim.Cloche: Cloche is French for 'bell'. These close-fitting bell-shaped hats were a signature of 1920s flappers.
Hats with a brim.Beanie: A beanie is a brimless knit cap, and its name probably comes from 'bean', old slang for the head. It sits close to the skull.
Hats with a brim.Beret: The beret is a round, soft, flat cap with no brim, worn by Basque shepherds and later by soldiers and artists.
Hats with a brim.Fez: The fez is a brimless felt cap shaped like a truncated cone, named after the Moroccan city of Fez.
Hats with a brim.Turban: A turban is a long cloth wound around the head, so it has no brim. Sikh men wear it as a part of faith.
Hats with a brim.Balaclava: The balaclava covers the head and neck. It's named for the Crimean War battle of Balaclava, where soldiers wore knitted caps against the cold.
Hats with a brim.Skullcap: A skullcap fits snugly on the crown of the head with no brim. It is worn by many religious groups.
Hats with a brim.Tam: A tam, or tam o'shanter, is a Scottish bonnet that sits flat on the head. The name comes from a poem by Robert Burns.
Hats with a brim.Kippah: The kippah, or yarmulke, is a small cap worn by Jewish men. It has no brim, so it doesn't fit.
Hats with a brim.Headscarf: A headscarf is cloth tied over the hair for warmth, modesty or style. It lacks the stiff brim that defines these hats.
Hats with a brim.Pillbox hat: The pillbox is a small, flat-topped hat with no brim, made famous by Jackie Kennedy in the 1960s.
Hats with a brim.Tiara: A tiara is a jeweled ornament worn on the head at formal occasions. It is a decoration, not a hat, and has no brim.
Hats with a brim.Crown: A crown is a ceremonial headpiece of metal and jewels with points or arches. It has no brim, and isn't a hat in the usual sense.
Hats with a brim.Headband: A headband is a strip of fabric or plastic that holds hair back, and it has no brim, so it fails to shade the face.

Traditional Indian garments.Sari: Draped in one unstitched length, the sari is one of the oldest garments still worn, with mentions dating back thousands of years.
Traditional Indian garments.Kurta: This long, loose shirt reaches the knees or below and comes in regional styles worn by men and women across South Asia.
Traditional Indian garments.Dhoti: This long cloth is wrapped round the waist and often pleated and tucked between the legs, traditional male wear in much of India.
Traditional Indian garments.Sherwani: A long, buttoned coat, it is popular as groom's wear at Indian weddings and is the more formal cousin of the kurta.
Traditional Indian garments.Lehenga: A bridal favourite, this ornate flared skirt is worn with a short blouse and long scarf, especially in Rajasthan and Gujarat.
Traditional Indian garments.Salwar kameez: The name means tunic and trousers, and the outfit comes from Punjab before it spread through South Asia.
Traditional Indian garments.Dupatta: This long scarf is draped over a shoulder or the head, and in many communities wearing it shows modesty and respect.
Traditional Indian garments.Nehru jacket: Jawaharlal Nehru, India's first prime minister, made this fitted, high-collared jacket his signature, and it became globally known.
Traditional Indian garments.Lungi: A checked or striped cloth wrapped around the waist like a skirt, the lungi is common in southern India and nearby countries.
Traditional Indian garments.Churidar: Tight trousers that bunch in folds near the ankle, churidar literally means bangle, after those wrinkles.
Traditional Indian garments.Kimono: Japan's wraparound robe is closed left over right, since right over left is reserved for dressing the dead.
Traditional Indian garments.Hanbok: Korea's traditional dress pairs a short jacket with a high-waisted skirt, and its sweeping curve echoes the roofs of old houses.
Traditional Indian garments.Qipao: A close-fitting dress from China, with a high collar and side slits, it became a fashion in 1920s Shanghai.
Traditional Indian garments.Ao dai: Vietnam's national dress is a long, slit tunic worn over trousers, and its name literally means long shirt.
Traditional Indian garments.Dirndl: This Alpine dress from Bavaria and Austria has a tradition that the apron bow's side shows if its wearer is single or taken.
Traditional Indian garments.Kilt: The tartan kilt is from Scotland, where every clan has its own pattern, and it has no tie to India.
Traditional Indian garments.Poncho: The poncho comes from the Andes, and the name is from Mapuche, an indigenous language of Chile.
Traditional Indian garments.Kaftan: A kaftan comes from Persia and the Ottoman world, so while it looks like many Indian garments, its roots lie elsewhere.
Traditional Indian garments.Dashiki: This bright West African shirt takes its name from a Yoruba word, and in 1960s America it was worn as a sign of pride.
Traditional Indian garments.Lederhosen: Lederhosen are leather shorts with suspenders, worn in Bavaria, and have nothing to do with Indian dress.
Traditional Indian garments.Serape: The serape is a long woven Mexican blanket-shawl, and the one with bright stripes is the one everyone pictures.
Traditional Indian garments.Thobe: This ankle-length robe from the Arab world is worn throughout the Gulf, and its name comes from the Arabic word for garment.
Traditional Indian garments.Barong: The barong Tagalog is a sheer embroidered Filipino shirt, worn untucked, and a legend says Spanish colonizers required this so Filipinos could not hide weapons.
Traditional Indian garments.Toga: The toga was a Roman wool drape for citizens only, which puts it far from Indian garments.

Italian fashion houses.Gucci: Founded in Florence in 1921 as a saddlery and leather goods shop, Gucci became a global luxury giant famed for its double-G logo.
Italian fashion houses.Prada: Miuccia Prada, the founder's granddaughter, has a PhD in political science, and her black nylon backpack in the 1980s made the house a trendsetter.
Italian fashion houses.Versace: Gianni Versace's Medusa head logo was chosen because it mesmerised, and he was murdered in 1997 in Miami Beach.
Italian fashion houses.Armani: Giorgio Armani rose from a window dresser at La Rinascente to a billionaire, and he made the soft, unstructured suit a global icon.
Italian fashion houses.Valentino: Valentino Garavani's signature shade is a vivid red, called Valentino red, which he used in his earliest collections.
Italian fashion houses.Dolce & Gabbana: Domenico Dolce and Stefano Gabbana started their label in Milan in 1985, and Sicily has been a constant source of inspiration for them.
Italian fashion houses.Fendi: Rome's Fendi began as a fur and leather shop, and Karl Lagerfeld designed for it for more than fifty years.
Italian fashion houses.Moschino: Founded in 1983 by Franco Moschino, this Milan house is known for cheeky, satirical designs that poke fun at fashion itself.
Italian fashion houses.Bottega Veneta: Its slogan 'when your own initials are enough' captures this house, which has no logo and is known for woven leather.
Italian fashion houses.Missoni: The Missoni family built an empire on zigzag knit patterns that began as a small knitting workshop near Milan.
Italian fashion houses.Ferragamo: Salvatore Ferragamo made shoes for Hollywood stars in the 1920s before returning to Italy and building his own brand.
Italian fashion houses.Chanel: Gabrielle Chanel, a French designer, launched No. 5 in 1921, and the house is Parisian.
Italian fashion houses.Dior: Christian Dior's 1947 New Look, with nipped waist and full skirt, made Paris the capital of fashion again after the war.
Italian fashion houses.Hermès: Hermès began as a harness workshop in Paris in 1837, and the Birkin bag is named after actress Jane Birkin.
Italian fashion houses.Louis Vuitton: Louis Vuitton started in Paris in 1854 making trunks, and his monogram canvas was used in part to deter copying.
Italian fashion houses.Givenchy: Hubert de Givenchy was close to Audrey Hepburn, and designed the little black dress she wore in Breakfast at Tiffany's.
Italian fashion houses.Balenciaga: Cristobal Balenciaga was Spanish, but he moved to Paris, which is why the house is French.
Italian fashion houses.Burberry: Thomas Burberry invented gabardine in 1879, and the British house is famous for its trench coat and check.
Italian fashion houses.Ralph Lauren: Ralph Lauren was born Ralph Lifshitz in the Bronx, and he built an American empire on preppy polo shirts.
Italian fashion houses.Calvin Klein: Calvin Klein is American and made its name in the 1980s with provocative jeans and underwear ads.
Italian fashion houses.Yves Saint Laurent: Yves Saint Laurent, who was only 21 when he took over Dior, is French, and the house in question is Parisian.
Italian fashion houses.Lacoste: Founded by tennis star René Lacoste, nicknamed the Crocodile, this French brand put an animal logo on the shirt first.
Italian fashion houses.Celine: Founded by Celine Vipiana in 1945 in Paris, this house began with children's shoes.
Italian fashion houses.Tommy Hilfiger: Tommy Hilfiger is American, and he started in the 1980s with preppy style and a red, white and blue logo.

Parts of a classic pirate costume.Eye patch: A popular theory says it kept one eye adjusted to darkness for fighting below deck, though no one can prove that.

Parts of a classic pirate costume.Hook hand: Captain Hook from J.M. Barrie's 1904 play Peter Pan made the hook famous; real pirates rarely had one.
Parts of a classic pirate costume.Peg leg: Long John Silver in Stevenson's 1883 Treasure Island helped cement the image, along with a crutch.
Parts of a classic pirate costume.Parrot: Long John Silver's parrot, Captain Flint, squawked Pieces of eight! in Treasure Island.
Parts of a classic pirate costume.Cutlass: A short, curved sword that suited cramped ships, where a long blade would get in the way.
Parts of a classic pirate costume.Sash: Often used to stash pistols, since flintlocks took a long time to reload.
Parts of a classic pirate costume.Knee-high boots: Sailors usually worked barefoot for better grip on slippery decks, so boots are mostly theater.
Parts of a classic pirate costume.Gold earring: Legend says it paid for a burial if the pirate's body washed ashore.
Parts of a classic pirate costume.Tutu: A ballerina skirt; classic ones can have many layers of stiffened tulle.
Parts of a classic pirate costume.Tiara: The word tiara was used for the ancient Persian headdress.
Parts of a classic pirate costume.Halo: The halo in art goes back to ancient sun-god images, long before Christian saints.
Parts of a classic pirate costume.Stethoscope: Invented in 1816 by Rene Laennec, who used a rolled-up paper tube to listen to a patient.
Parts of a classic pirate costume.Magic wand: Stage magicians use wands to draw the audience's eyes away from the real trick.
Parts of a classic pirate costume.Space helmet: Apollo helmet visors had a thin gold coating to reflect harsh sunlight.
Parts of a classic pirate costume.Bunny ears: The Playboy Club's bunny costume debuted in 1960.
Parts of a classic pirate costume.Lab coat: White coats show spills and contamination, which is why chemists adopted them.
Parts of a classic pirate costume.Tool belt: Batman's utility belt is the superhero version of this work belt.
Parts of a classic pirate costume.Hard hat: Invented in 1919 by Edward Bullard, from his father's miner hats; Golden Gate Bridge crews were required to wear them in the 1930s.
Parts of a classic pirate costume.Ballet slippers: Pointe shoes can wear out after a single performance for professional dancers.
Parts of a classic pirate costume.Fairy wings: Victorian fairy painters drew them with butterfly or dragonfly wings.
Parts of a classic pirate costume.Fake fangs: Bela Lugosi's 1931 Dracula famously wore no fangs on screen.
Parts of a classic pirate costume.Pom-poms: The first cheerleaders, in the 1880s, were all men.

Places inside Hogwarts castle.Owlery: A tower at the top of the castle where post owls roost; students send letters and parcels from here.
Places inside Hogwarts castle.Trophy Room: A corridor display of awards where Tom Riddle's Special Services to the School medal was found, Harry noticing his name there.
Places inside Hogwarts castle.Moving staircases: The castle has 142 staircases, and many of them move on a Friday or so, which is why first-years get lost.
Places inside Hogwarts castle.Restricted Section: Library books too dangerous for ordinary students need a teacher's signed note; Harry sneaks in under his Invisibility Cloak.

Places inside Hogwarts castle.Gringotts: The goblin-run wizard bank sits in Diagon Alley, guarded by dragons deep in its vaults, far from the school.
Places inside Hogwarts castle.Azkaban: The wizard prison on a North Sea island is guarded by Dementors, not part of the castle.
Places inside Hogwarts castle.Ministry of Magic: This government sits below London and is entered through a red telephone box; it's nowhere near the school.
Places inside Hogwarts castle.Knockturn Alley: A shady side street off Diagon Alley selling dark objects like the Hand of Glory; it's not inside Hogwarts.
Places inside Hogwarts castle.Hogsmeade: The only all-wizard village in Britain lies near the school, and third-years may visit; it's outside the castle.
Places inside Hogwarts castle.Privet Drive: Number four is where the Dursleys live in Surrey, a Muggle street far from any magic.
Places inside Hogwarts castle.Godric's Hollow: The village where Harry's parents died, and where Godric Gryffindor was born; it is not in the castle.
Places inside Hogwarts castle.The Burrow: The Weasleys' crooked, many-storied home in Ottery St Catchpole; it is far from Hogwarts.
Places inside Hogwarts castle.Leaky Cauldron: A London pub and inn that is the entrance to Diagon Alley; Muggles can't even see it.
Places inside Hogwarts castle.Shrieking Shack: Supposedly the most haunted building in Britain, it's in Hogsmeade, not at the castle; it's where Lupin transformed.
Places inside Hogwarts castle.Grimmauld Place: Number twelve is Sirius Black's family home in London, and the headquarters of the Order of the Phoenix.
Places inside Hogwarts castle.St Mungo's: The wizard hospital for magical maladies is in London, whereas Hogwarts uses its own infirmary.
Places inside Hogwarts castle.Honeydukes: A Hogsmeade sweet shop with Fizzing Whizbees and chocolate frogs, but it's in the village, not the castle.

Counties of Ireland (not England).Devon: An English county famous for cream teas, where the cream goes on the scone first, or so Devon's tradition insists.

Counties of Ireland (not England).Cornwall: Its own Celtic language, Cornish, was revived after dying out as a community language, and the county is famed for pasties.

Counties of Ireland (not England).Norfolk: English county of the Broads, a network of man-made waterways created by medieval peat digging that later flooded.

Counties of Ireland (not England).Yorkshire: England's largest historic county, so big it was split into Ridings, and not part of Ireland.
Counties of Ireland (not England).Fife: A trap: Fife is a Scottish council area, not English or Irish, and is home to St Andrews, the home of golf.
Counties of Ireland (not England).Cheshire: English county tied to Lewis Carroll's Cheshire Cat, and to its famous crumbly cheese.
Counties of Ireland (not England).Cumbria: English county containing the Lake District and Scafell Pike, England's highest peak at 978 metres.
Counties of Ireland (not England).Rutland: England's smallest historic county, with the manmade Rutland Water reservoir. It is not in Ireland.
